Episode 2 – The Title Decider , the latest instalment of the 2026 FIM SuperSide docu-series presented by Marin, is now available. Covering the final three rounds of the FIM Sidecar World Championship, it takes viewers inside the championship battle as the season builds towards its decisive weekend at Oschersleben, Germany .
Harrison Payne and Kevin Rousseau emerged as the 2026 Marin FIM Sidecar World Champions , reclaiming the crown they first won together in 2024. The British/French pairing secured the title with victory in Saturday’s Sprint race, then completed their season in style by dominating Sunday’s Main race for their ninth win of the campaign.
Behind them, the contest for the remaining medals brought another compelling storyline. Defending champions Sam and Thomas Christie secured silver , while Pekka Päivärinta and Adam Christie took bronze .
With exclusive access to riders, teams and the paddock, Episode 2 goes beyond the results to reveal the pressure, preparation and strategy behind the racing. Behind-the-scenes footage and interviews capture the emotions of the closing rounds, from the pursuit of crucial championship points to the celebrations as the crown is secured.
It is an opportunity to relive the decisive action and discover the people and stories behind a memorable championship finale.
Full coverage of rounds three, five and six of the 2026 FIM Sidecar World Championship – along with behind-the-scenes footage, interviews and expert analysis – are available on FIM-MOTO.TV. For more details click here .

Will Coleman and Very Dignified. Photo by Hannah Cole Photography.
The USA now owns two of the top three spots on the FEI Eventing World Athlete Rankings after the October points update. Now joining Boyd Martin in the top three is Will Coleman, who’s seventh-place finish at Burghley contributed to his jump from seventh last month to third in the world. New Zealand’s Tim Price retains the World #1 title and stands to head into the off-season as the titleholder with a strong performance at Pau later this month.
Points for these rankings are calculated on a rolling 12 month period. An athlete’s best six results count, so you could be cycling in fresh points with good results (the higher the level and, of course, the higher the placing, the more points you earn) as last year’s points roll off. You can read more on how the world ranking points are tabulated here .
There are a total of three U.S. riders in the top 10, with Caroline Pamukcu rising from 12th into sixth with her podium finish at Burghley last month.

articles.title_orig: Dow futures slide 300 points as yields continue rising; oil surges 5%: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures slide 300 points as yields continue rising; oil surges 5%: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures were lower on Thursday as investors faced more pressure from rising Treasury yields and elevated oil prices.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures fell 347 points, or 0.7%. S&P 500 futures dipped 0.4%, and Nasdaq-100 futures were 0.6% lower.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield rose more than 5 basis points to 5.331%, around levels not seen since 2002. The 30-year Treasury bond yield also traded near 24-year highs at 5.702% after rising more than 4 basis points. Those moves came after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said more hikes may be needed to curb inflation.
Oil prices spiked also after President Donald Trump said he doesn't want to make a deal with Iran to end the war, while the U.S. is reportedly preparing for " massive bombing " in the Middle East. Brent crude jumped 4% to around $104 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate futures , meanwhile, advanced 4% to around $92.
Key areas of the market sensitive to higher borrowing costs such as banks and technology were under pressure yet again. Intel and Marvell Technology shares were each down more than 2%, while Bank of America and Citigroup shed around 1%.
Yields and oil have stoked volatility in equities of late, as concern grows that higher energy prices will keep inflation elevated and force the Federal Reserve to further raise rates.
Many investors are maintaining an optimistic view of the stock market, however. They expect that the start of earnings season could give the market the fuel it needs for the next leg higher.
In the third quarter, the S&P 500 is expected post a blended earnings growth rate of roughly 30%, which would be a third straight quarter of above-25% earnings growth, according to FactSet.
"If earnings remain strong, and the idea is that they probably will, if expectations are met and/or higher, that is going to sustain this rally — despite the fact that rates are higher," Courtney Garcia, senior wealth advisor at Payne Capital Management, told CNBC's " Closing Bell ." "It's not going to derail the market."
Palantir Technologies was one of the few stocks trading higher on Thursday, with shares gaining 2% after the name received an upgrade at Goldman Sachs . The firm called for more upside ahead as the total addressable market could be "setting up for another step function change" as a result of the shift to sovereign AI and bespoke applications.
Across the Atlantic, the pan-European Stoxx 600 was 0.85% lower in morning trade. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 was 0.44% down, while France's CAC 40 shed 0.81%. The German DAX dipped 0.77%, as Italy's FTSE MIB shed 0.98%.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 1.42% lower, while South Korea's Kospi dropped 2.62%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.77%, and mainland China's CSI 300 declined 1.09%.
Initial unemployment claims edged lower last week, continuing the trend of a low layoff environment, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
First-time filings for jobless benefits totaled a seasonally adjusted 197,000 for the week ended Oct. 3, down 2,000 from the prior period and just below the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 200,000.
Continuing claims, which run a week behind, rose by 17,000 to 1.72 million.
Goldman Sachs upgraded military software and analytics firm Palantir on Thursday to a buy rating from neutral.
The investment bank raised its price target on the stock to $230, implying 18.5% upside. Shares closed Wednesday at price of $194.12.
Goldman sees more government contracts, more automated workers and a more vertical supply chain in the company's future.
"The [total addressable market] may be setting up for another step function change in depth, because of the shift to sovereign AI, bespoke applications, and Palantir's newer verticalization strategy," Goldman analyst Gabriela Borges wrote in a Thursday note.
"The [forward deployed engineer] model is more than simply hiring FDEs; it requires tight feedback loops between field and product, which Palantir has perfected to the point of being able to automate via AI FDEs," she added.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise benchmark interest rates, though he isn't sure of a timetable or the degree to which it will need to happen.
"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal. But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur," Waller said during a speech in Turkey. "The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
In addition to his remarks on rates, the policymaker offered a defense of forward guidance, saying it can serve as an effective "signaling" tool for the Fed's expectations on where it should set rates.
Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket:
"Markets may have to climb a renewed wall of worry to set fresh records, but waiting for these concerns to fade could mean missing further gains. We believe investors should focus less on finding a perfect entry point and more on maintaining exposure while managing concentration and timing risks through a disciplined portfolio approach," Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO of the Americas at UBS, said in a note.
U.S. Treasury yields climbed higher on Thursday ahead of a closely watched long-dated bond auction later.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was 4 basis points higher at 5.322%, after reaching its highest level since 2002 on Wednesday before retreating later in the day. The 30-year Treasury bond yield rose over 4 basis points to 5.705%, after trading just below a 24-year high in the previous session. The 2-year Treasury note yield was nearly 3 basis points up to 4.793%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Asia markets closed lower Thursday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 ending 1.42% lower at 69,042.11, and the broader Topix dropping 1.51% to 4,091.46.
South Korea's Kospi fell 2.62% to 6,625.93, while the small- and mid-cap Kosdaq lost 0.69% to 892.27.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.77% to 8,660.90.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was down 1.43% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 1.09% lower at 4,310.28
The Governor of the Bank of France Emmanuel Moulin said Thursday that European inflation is "100%" driven by energy, adding that the geopolitical shock is now feeding into a financial shock.
As yields on French government debt surged to multiyear highs amid broader concerns over fiscal pressures in several European countries, the European Central Bank board member highlighted a "strong correlation" between oil, long-term U.S. interest rates and rates in Europe.
However, Moulin added that he does not envisage second-round effects.
Meanwhile, fellow ECB board member and president of the Dutch central bank Olaf Sleijpen said medium- to long-term inflation expectations remain "well anchored."
Stoxx 50 futures were down 0.35% ahead of Thursday's trading session, with Europe's major bourses in mixed territory prior to the market open.
The French CAC 40 was seen 0.06% lower, and Germany's DAX was down 0.27%, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 was off by 0.14%
The Italian FTSE MIB was also in negative territory, down 0.56%.
European stock markets started Thursday's session lower, with regional sectors and major bourses seen moving into negative territory in early trade.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.07% lower shortly after 8:00 a.m. in London (3:00 a.m. E.T.).
In London, the U.K.'s FTSE 100 was down 0.81%, while the French CAC 40 fell 0.85% in Paris. Elsewhere, Germany's DAX dropped 1.08% in Frankfurt. The Italian FTSE MIB was 1.53% lower in Milan.
The continent's oil and gas names were the sole bright spot, advancing 0.32%, as all other sectors turned red. Basic resources led losses, sliding 2.02%, with European banks down 1.82% and healthcare stocks falling 1.45%

articles.title_orig: The 10 Least Sustainable Countries In The World
articles.title_zh: The 10 Least Sustainable Countries In The World
articles.content_orig:
Each year, the Environmental Performance Index (EPI) releases its report . This story focuses on the 2026 edition and, with a few exceptions, draws primarily on that report. It examines the bottom 10 of the 177 nations ranked.
The scores are built from metrics covering environmental health and protection. The data are divided into 12 categories, including air quality, forests, fisheries, and climate, and draw on information from international agreements. The index also leans heavily on the OECD handbook, which was created to guide the construction of composite indicators from data and policy measures.
The ratings rest on three main pillars :
Ecosystem health (45%) , which evaluates wildlife habitat, forests, fisheries, and farming.
Climate change (30%) , which is driven largely by greenhouse gas emissions and whether they are rising or falling.
Human health (25%) , which is built from data on air pollution, drinking water, and sanitation.
In the authors' words, "These indicators provide a gauge at a national scale of how close countries are to established environmental policy targets." They hope the index will help governments set better policy on sustainability practices, laws, and regulations.
Scores can range from 0 to 100, with 100 being the best. In practice, the top score belongs to Estonia at 74.79, followed closely by Luxembourg at 74.24.
The 10 nations at the bottom of the list tend to share several traits. One is unhealthy air and water, both of which cause major health problems; India and Laos score particularly poorly on this measure. Another is rising greenhouse gas emissions in most of these countries. India illustrates the trend: according to World Population Review, it ranks second only to China in coal consumption. Finally, poor ecosystem health drags down scores, owing to farm pollution runoff, overfishing, and a lack of government protection for land.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of new pro sports team ETFs lead world of retail investing to the edge of gambling
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of new pro sports team ETFs lead world of retail investing to the edge of gambling
articles.content_orig:
In 1989, all-time hits leader Pete Rose was banned from Major League Baseball for life because of his gambling activities. He wasn't reinstated until last year, months after his death in 2024.
Fast-forward to today, and Pete Rose's gambling might seem like just another day on Wall Street as financial firms expand the ways fans can put money behind their teams, beyond a beer and a $15 hot dog.
You may soon be able to buy a ticker for your favorite hockey team, and it isn't a stake in the franchise. Multiple asset managers have filed to launch dozens of ETFs, one for every NHL team, with MLB baseball team funds filed as well, all built on new futures contracts that track a team's season statistics. None has begun trading but in all, hundreds of ETFs that track the single-season performance of one professional team across a mix of statistical categories have been filed at the SEC for approval.
Some finance experts see the development as lacking any nuance whatsoever.
"The line between gambling and investing has not simply been blurred, it has been erased," said Robert Johnson, a professor of finance at Creighton University.
Among fund companies getting in on the novel trend are VolatilityShares , LeagueShares, Roundhill Investments , and Rex Financial .
None of the four companies responded to requests for comment. Asset managers typically cannot publicly comment during the period between when funds are filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval and when they become effective, if approved.
Rex, a Miami-based ETF issuer, announced Sept. 21 that it was launching Alpha Sports Holdings, a new subsidiary built to turn team performance into exchange-traded funds. REX has filed with the SEC for BaseballShares and HockeyShares, suites of ETFs that would track Major League Baseball and National Hockey League teams through futures contracts that CME Group, the derivatives exchange, lists on indexes built by FutureSports, an index company. The underlying CME futures , which began trading for NHL teams in late September, need to first establish a trading history.
Each team's index opens the season at a set number and moves as the team racks up statistics, including runs scored, stolen bases and strikeouts for baseball, then resets in the offseason.
"The sports industry generates hundreds of billions of dollars a year, but there has never been a liquid, transparent investment product tied directly to what happens in live games," said Greg King, CEO of Alpha Sports, in a press release. "Alpha Sports exists to build that product for passionate investors who want to participate in the fortunes of their favorite teams."
Johnson, though, said the sports-themed ETFs are far more gaming than investing.
"I thought that the ETF world had jumped the shark with the introduction of the 2X and 3X leveraged and inverse ETFs. In my mind these were simply vehicles for short term speculators. But, at least these vehicles were based upon assets. The new structures — and I call them structures, not assets — are simply gambling dressed up as investing," Johnson said.
In fact, the proposed team ETFs include in some cases leveraged versions of trades on single-team performance.
The boom in prediction markets is already blurring the lines between sports wagering and market trading. Unlike prediction markets contracts, the sports team ETFs are tracking futures off an index rather than a single event (e.g. win or loss). But while structurally contracts in this market have a role to play for investors, in the case of sports performance, Johnson says the case is weak.
"They have societal value in that parties are able to hedge natural positions and transact with other speculators willing to bear that risk. This allows a more optimal allocation of risk," Johnson said.
But he added that is not the case when individual investors are making bets on the performance of sports teams they follow.
"There are no natural positions being hedged. In the aggregate, they destroy wealth," Johnson said.
Here's a look at other stories offering insight on ETFs for investors.
Alex Michalka, vice president of investment research at investing platform Wealthfront, said the case for investing in the performance of sports teams is nearly impossible to separate from gambling, since wagering on whether a sports team will win or lose does not facilitate an economic purpose that adds value to the world.
"That is not to say a legitimate economic use case is impossible, but most people will likely use these funds for the same reasons they place a sports bet, which is often to show loyalty to a team or simply for entertainment," Michalka said. "Just because sports betting has an ETF wrapper, it does not change the risk associated with it," Michalka added.
Futures have long been used for hedging, and the CME contracts and FutureSports may be ways for sponsors, broadcasters, insurers and arena vendors to potentially hedge exposure against assets and liabilities. Conceptually, that's similar to an airline hedging fuel prices or an insurer hedging extreme weather risks. But in actuality, that does not apply to the vast majority of investors when it comes to these specific sports investments.
"Sports as an asset class exists, but for a few very select people out there," said Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas. "I'm unsure if 'democratizing' really makes sense here," he said.
He added there are also many risks when it comes to novel ETFs like these with so few buyers in the market with a justifiable economic reason to trade them, risks that range from liquidity to price discovery and manipulation. Insider trading around injuries, trades, and coaching changes; and illiquidity in the investments during the offseason, up to four months of no activity, though trades and free agency can impact outlook, are among them. There should also be the expectations for wide bid/ask spreads and market imbalances with "fan enthusiasm driving prices and no commercial hedgers," Baird Strategas wrote in a preliminary analysis.
Despite the risks, all of which are covered in risk disclosures within these ETFs' prospectuses, Nate Geraci, an ETF expert and president of NovaDius Wealth Management, expects them to be approved by the SEC. Assuming the futures contracts "function properly, and establish sufficient liquidity, I don't see a regulatory reason why the SEC wouldn't approve the ETFs. CME-traded futures held in an ETF wrapper certainly aren't novel, though it's entirely possible the SEC could attempt to classify these sports-focused ETFs as such," he said.
The SEC is currently in the midst of a rulemaking proposal and public comment period covering "novel" ETFs, a move the regulator made after ETF companies filed for prediction markets ETFs.
Geraci is not surprised that ETF issuers are chasing the concept. "It's somewhat ironic that ETFs began as a way to offer low-cost, broad-based exposure to the market and have morphed in recent years into expensive, narrowly focused speculation vehicles. That said, it's a tale as old as time in asset management, where fund issuers rush to package and sell whatever is capturing investors' attention," he said.
Evan Mills, a financial advisor at Scholar Advising, an independent fee-only advisory firm, said it is important to understand the difference between owning a productive asset and making a bet on an outcome.
"If you're buying stock in a business, that stock is tied to revenue, earnings, and cash flow, so it appreciates based on that, as well as demand for the stock," Mills said. Bonds, meanwhile, include a contractual stream of payments, and that's how you make money off them.
When you put these sports teams under a ticker symbol, it can add a veneer of credibility, but he said it is still just speculation. "And where speculation really hurts is when those two things get tied together both financially and emotionally, which usually happens in retirement funds or portfo

articles.title_orig: Early Treatment Support and Real-World Care Gaps
articles.title_zh: Early Treatment Support and Real-World Care Gaps
articles.content_orig:
This episode maps the early weeks of oral zongertinib and the real-world factors that threaten them.
This episode maps the early weeks of oral zongertinib and the real-world factors that threaten them. The panel describes a model in which a clinical pharmacist calls the patient at home to confirm the drug has arrived and review administration, followed by an early advanced practice provider visit with labs, a second visit shortly after, and body imaging within the first few months. Faculty explain how community practices without an embedded thoracic pharmacist can replicate this through pharmacotherapy referrals, virtual visits, and phone outreach, and how pharmacists catch dosing nuances such as weight-based dosing and drug interactions. The discussion then examines why patients stop therapy outside trials, from distance and transportation barriers to unprepared reactions to low-grade diarrhea, and dispels the idea that dose reduction sacrifices efficacy. The episode closes on fragmented community care, where the time from diagnosis to drug in hand can stretch past a month.

articles.title_orig: Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
articles.title_zh: Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
articles.content_orig:
Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.
The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.
The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia.
Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens."
She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour."
Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring.

articles.title_orig: Going analog in algorithmic world
articles.title_zh: Going analog in algorithmic world
articles.content_orig:
Abby Brown, a 22-year-old crafter, finds Pinterest to be “AI slop.”
She recalls scrolling through the social media platform for inspiration in the past, but now she’s disenchanted by the surge of AI-generated images. It has turned her off from spending time online. Brown now finds herself reaching for her knitting needles.
“It makes me value handmade work more because I know a person spent a considerable amount of time making it,” she says.
Brown is part of a wave of young people who are starting to embrace analog hobbies—from knitting and pottery to film photography and risograph printing—as technology, artificial intelligence in particular, becomes increasingly ingrained in everyday life. Across Rochester, artists, business owners, and hobbyists say the appeal of analog isn’t nostalgia, but the ability to slow down and physically create something.
For many, it starts with what AI can’t offer: the meaning that comes from making something by hand.
Shelby Przybylek, owner of Little Button Craft, has witnessed that desire for meaningful art firsthand.
Over the last few years, she watched younger customers flock to crafting meetups, where they knit, crochet, or do other types of fiber arts.
Beyond simply seeking a human touch, Przybylek observes, many are turning to these tactile activities for their mental health benefits.
“People have really realized that it is a de-stressor, and you can really find some happiness when you’re making something with your hands,” she says.
Przybylek explains that bilateral integration —the brain’s ability to coordinate both sides of the body through efficient communication between the left and right hemispheres—sends chemicals to the brain that produce feelings of happiness and calm.
“When you’re working with your hands, it’s very calming—even if you make something that’s not perfect, it’s rewarding,” Przybylek says.
An increasingly popular way to create by hand is the art of pottery. A recently opened studio, Laurentide Clay , shows how pottery lets artists disconnect from screens. Terry O’Brien, the studio’s administrative coordinator, says he and other founders noticed a resurgence of interest in ceramics during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
“There is something about being isolated and online that can feel a bit unnatural, at least to me,” he told the Beacon recently. He describes it as a question of offsetting an increasingly digital lifestyle with a craft that requires total focus. “I think it’s just establishing a balance in people’s lives.”
Kyle Lascelle, who oversees the studio’s educational programs, agreed with O’Brien, adding, “You have clay all over your hands, and so it’s difficult to be on your phone.”
The growing presence of algorithms has impacted people’s shopping habits. Sources for this article say many people are more intentional about who they support, encouraging them to seek out handmade products from real artists instead of machine-made graphics.
The desire for a more relaxed pace and to find analog ways to be creative isn’t limited to knitting, sewing, or even pottery. At Scott’s Photo, Tatiana Ariola has watched young people embrace another slower medium: film photography.
“The draw to film is the tangibility,” Ariola explains. “You can touch your negatives … they exist.”
Unlike digital photography, film photos cannot be readily altered.
“People are very much happier with film because it’s not edited,” explains Ariola. “You can always go back to the negative and know what was real.”
Unlike smartphone or digital cameras that can capture dozens of images in seconds, a roll of film offers just 24 or 36 exposures, making every photograph an intentional choice. In addition, many people today have grown accustomed to instant gratification, where photos are immediately available to see, edit, and post.
By using analog cameras, the photographer has to finish the roll of film, which then must be developed and the images printed.
“I think there’s a lot more intentionality (compared with) digital, where you can just spray and pray, take as many photos as you can, and hope that one comes out right,” Ariola says. “You can’t do that with film.”
Finding joy in the irregularities is what makes analog hobbies special.
“When you see an imperfection, you know (that) definitely a human made this,” says Brown.
For Evan Bobrow at Rathaus Press, a risograph printing business, imperfections are what make a risograph, a combination of screen printing and photocopying, distinct from other printing methods.
“​​There will always be misregistration,” Bobrow says. “There will always be some level of smudging or different levels of coverage, and yeah, a lot of people are interested in that. That it makes it feel like more of a handmade object.”
He believes the desire to go analog is human and tactile.
“I think knowing that whoever made something made a really intentional choice to make it physical can make that connection feel more special,” he says.
Brown says knitting gives her an intentional reason to step away from screens that increasingly overpower work, school, and social life.
At the same time, social media has helped bring more attention to those crafts.
“I think it’s helped introduce more people to film photography, and to get people information to improve their photography, and it’s also a platform to share your work,” Ariola says.
“I think that it’s very good for the people who are trying to get into crafting to see what the process is like before they have to buy all of the products and try on their own,” she says.
For Brown, crafting isn’t just something to do alone. It’s become a way to meet people outside of work, school, and social media. After graduating from Rochester Institute of Technology, she’s been searching for third spaces —places beyond home and work where people can create genuine communities and connections.
Little Button Craft hosts Fiber Nights at Abundance Food Co-op every Wednesday (except the second Wednesday of the month) from 6-8 p.m. Przybylek hopes that attendees will use those weekly meetings to de-stress and be among their crafty peers. Alongside Fiber Nights, she wants to keep offering low-cost courses for people seeking to get into art.
“I think it’s being brave and creating that third space for people, because they will come, they will very much come,” she says.
Przybylek has noticed that some of those who religiously attend Fiber Night events have created their own friend groups and then meet up to do crafts together.
“They’re forming this beautiful friendship that started with crafting,” she says.
Scott’s Photo is aiming to become a third space for film photographers, a community hub where people can learn from each other and share their work, Ariola says. The store has been hosting monthly photo walks at various locations in the city and beyond.
Rathaus Press has open hours for creatives to come in and use its facilities. Bobrow describes the setting as a collaborative space for people to create art.
“Art (can) be something that’s very personal, but I think it’s also really important for it to be a communal experience,” he says.
Jacob Dambra, the community coordinator at Laurentide Clay, has noticed that various ceramic studios in Rochester provide a breeding ground for communities to form.
“So many people I know through ceramics have built most of their social network,” says Dambra. “It almost doesn’t make sense to do (ceramics) by yourself.”
This shift to analog isn’t unique to Rochester; it reflects what appears to be a national trend that has emerged in recent years, fed by a growing dissatisfaction with technology.
In a 2023 Harris Poll , a majority of Gen Z and millennial respondents (58% each) said they believe new technologies are more likely to drive people apart than bring them together. By contrast, fewer than half of older respondents — Gen Xers (48%) and boomers (47%) — responded that way. In the same survey, 80% of Gen Z respondents and 82% of millennials said t

articles.title_orig: MAYBELLINE NEW YORK LAUNCHES "TOGETHER WE'RE BRAVE" CAMPAIGN FOR WORLD MENTAL HEALTH DAY
articles.title_zh: MAYBELLINE NEW YORK LAUNCHES "TOGETHER WE'RE BRAVE" CAMPAIGN FOR WORLD MENTAL HEALTH DAY
articles.content_orig:
Maybelline's Brave Together Platform Introduces New Campaign That Spotlights the Power of Connection and Support in Mental Health Journeys
NEW YORK , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ahead of World Mental Health Day on October 10, Maybelline New York unveiled "Together We're Brave," the latest chapter of Brave Together, the brand's global mental health program that has helped more than four million people access free one-to-one support worldwide. The campaign spotlights the unbreakable bonds that help people navigate anxiety, depression and other mental health challenges and celebrates the loved ones who stand beside them when they need it most.
With mental health challenges affecting more than just the individual experiencing them, loved ones often want to help but may not know where to start. Through "Together We're Brave," Maybelline New York aims to support the support system itself, equipping people with the awareness and encouragement needed to show up for those they care about. Through real-life, heartfelt stories featuring mothers and daughters, best friends and other meaningful duos, the campaign highlights the transformative role of connection while encouraging people to seek support for themselves or someone they care about.
"At Maybelline New York, we know that mental health journeys are rarely traveled alone," said Sandrine Jolly, Global Brand President, Maybelline New York. "With 'Together We're Brave,' we're expanding the conversation around mental health to also recognize the people who stand beside us during life's most challenging moments. By sharing these stories, we hope to inspire more open conversations and remind people that it is brave to reach out, whether for yourself or someone you care about."
Since launching in 2020, Brave Together has supported partnerships with more than 45 nonprofit organizations across 37 countries and contributed nearly $10 million toward mental health initiatives globally. Through "Together We're Brave," Maybelline New York continues its commitment to increasing awareness, reducing stigma and helping more people access the support they need. As part of this commitment, Maybelline New York will continue to work alongside the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) to raise awareness, expand access to resources, and encourage conversations around mental health here in the U.S.
"When someone we care about is struggling, we may not always know the right thing to say — but showing up matters," said Christine Crawford, M.D., chief medical officer at NAMI. "Listening without judgment, staying connected, and helping someone find support can make a real difference. Through our work with Maybelline New York and Brave Together, we're reminding people that you don't need to have all the answers to be there for someone you love."
To learn more about Brave Together and how to access free mental health resources, visit www.maybelline.com/bravetogether .
About Maybelline New York Rooted in New York, Maybelline has always stood for self-expression, accessibility, and cultural relevance. From inventing modern mascara to becoming the No. 1 makeup brand in the world*, we have built global authority and trust by redefining traditional beauty standards in step with consumers' lives. Operating at the intersection of cosmopolitan culture, beauty trends, innovation, and creativity, we continue to open new possibilities by daring to invent what does not yet exist.
In 2020, Maybelline introduced Brave Together, a long-term program to support anxiety and depression worldwide. Brave Together provides critical one-on-one support, an online education hub, a variety of programming to help destigmatize the conversation around mental health and has committed to donate $20 million over the next five years to global and local organizations. For more information visit www.maybelline.com or www.maybelline.com/bravetogether .
*Source Euromonitor International Limited: Beauty and Personal Care 2026ed, retail value, RSP, all retail channels, 2011-2025 data.

articles.title_orig: EVERSANA and Pulse Infoframe Announce Strategic Partnership to Deliver Global Real-World Evidence and HEOR Solutions
articles.title_zh: EVERSANA and Pulse Infoframe Announce Strategic Partnership to Deliver Global Real-World Evidence and HEOR Solutions
articles.content_orig:
Collaboration creates unmatched capabilities in biopharma industry for real world data generation and insights for market access strategy
CHICAGO , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EVERSANA , a leading provider of technology enabled, modern commercialization services to the biopharmaceutical industry, today announced a strategic partnership with Pulse Infoframe, a leader in real-world evidence (RWE) generation and intelligence. Through the partnership, EVERSANA will pair its end-to-end commercialization, market access and health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) expertise with Pulse Infoframe's proprietary RWE platform and established evidence-generation capabilities, creating a single, continuous evidence engine for pharmaceutical and medical device companies.
The partnership spans the full arc of evidence generation: global site-network and feasibility assessments, registry and natural history study design, and direct data capture from sites and patients, followed by HTA-grade reporting, global value dossiers, and reimbursement strategy. By designing studies to serve regulators, HTA bodies, and commercial teams alike, EVERSANA and Pulse Infoframe help clients carry a single evidence base from first patient enrolled through launch and beyond.
"Real-world evidence has never been more critical as pharmaceutical companies work to develop the best strategies to bring innovative therapies to patients," said Mark Thierer, Chief Executive Officer, EVERSANA. "By pairing our deep commercial and health economics expertise with Pulse Infoframe's robust registry expertise in complex conditions, including rare disease and oncology, we can bring unmatched solutions to customers to help improve market access."
The partnership offers pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers a seamless solution for evidence generation from study design and global site-network assessments to sophisticated external control arm methods and Health Technology Assessment (HTA)-grade reporting. By uniting complementary strengths, the collaboration delivers compounding gains in efficiency, data quality, and global scale.
"Our platform was built to generate regulatory-grade evidence directly from sites and patients," said Femida Gwadry-Sridhar (PhD), Chief Executive Officer, Pulse Infoframe. "Working with EVERSANA connects that evidence to the regulatory, reimbursement, and commercial decisions it needs to support, at global scale."
The partnership will be highlighted by EVERSANA and Pulse Infoframe at ISPOR Europe 2026, November 8-11 in Vienna, Austria.
About EVERSANA ® EVERSANA ® is the leading independent provider of global services to the life sciences industry. The company's integrated solutions are rooted in the patient experience and span all stages of the product life cycle to deliver long-term, sustainable value for patients, prescribers, channel partners, and payers. The company serves more than 650 organizations, including innovative start-ups and established pharmaceutical companies, to advance life sciences solutions for a healthier world. To learn more about EVERSANA, visit eversana.com .
About Pulse Infoframe Pulse Infoframe is a leading real-world data and evidence generation partner that provides services to clients in the life sciences and healthcare sectors. The company owns and operates its real-world evidence platform, with expertise in registries, natural history studies, and the ability to generate regulatory-grade data directly from sites and patients.

articles.title_orig: The World is His Oyster
articles.title_zh: The World is His Oyster
articles.content_orig:
October 8, 2026 | Claire Hall
Seafood entrepreneur Keegan Jalbert is developing a new approach to oyster feed
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert, left, and his brother-in-law Bryan Zambrano are pictured on a boat as they visit an aquaculture farm in Ecuador, where they discussed feed trials using AccessFlora's proprietary omega-3 feed. Jalbert's startup is one of the finalists in next week's Wolff New Venture Competition (UConn Today).
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert ’23 (CLAS) ’27 MS has always been interested in agriculture, food, and innovation. Today he is finding new ways to grow oysters and share his love of seafood with customers who live far from the ocean.
Jalbert is the founder of AccessFlora , a sustainable aquaculture company with a proprietary omega-3 aquafeed for raising oysters in purified water at a hatchery. The outcome is a larger and healthier shellfish that isn’t confined to the coast nor dependent upon favorable ocean conditions.
“I think what keeps me going as an entrepreneur is that this work is very fun,’’ says Jalbert, who is pursuing a master’s degree in nutritional science. “My greatest motivation is the impact on how we source omega-3s as a critical nutrient for our human health and for agriculture. What’s helped me so much with the startup is that I love my work, and because of it I’ve developed great personal connections.’’
Startup to Compete in Wolff New Venture Championship
AccessFlora is one of five UConn-affiliated startups participating in the Wolff New Venture Competition next Tuesday, Oct. 13, at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford.
The competition, now in its 11th year, is hosted by the Connecticut Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation (CCEI) . The event will include awards of more than $150,000, including a $40,000 grand prize for the first-place finisher. Jalbert says whatever money AccessFlora wins will help ramp up production.
“In terms of shellfish farming, yes, what we’re doing is revolutionary,’’ Jalbert says. “Shellfish are not raised in land-based aquaculture because the omega-3 feed would be too expensive. On one hand, that makes shellfish really great, because they can grow out in the ocean without being fed and they are great for the environment. But on the other hand, this cultivation method takes a long time, it is labor intensive, and it is vulnerable to unpredictable ocean conditions. While our technology will not replace traditional shellfish farming, it does provide a highly resilient and quick way to raise oysters, independent of ocean access, allowing this to be done inland.’’
“The way that this technology works is that we have a healthy microalgae that we use to convert vinegar into omega-3 in controlled conditions, kind of like yeast turns sugars into alcohol,’’ Jalbert says. “This gives us a clean DHA omega-3, the nutrient that makes seafood such an important part in our diet.’’
But that’s just one step for the company.
“Our longer-term plan is for this to not just be raising oysters, but to be serving as an omega-3 source in enriched/fortified plant-based foods,’’ Jalbert says. “This is because that is a large market that our technology is really well suited for, especially now that the majority of U.S. population is deficient in omega-3.’’
Jalbert Brings Extensive Experience to His Work
Jalbert’s startup won the 2025 Innovation Quest competition at UConn and a $15,000 grand prize. He has partnered with professor Mingyu Qiao, in the Department of Nutritional Sciences in the College of Agriculture, Health and Natural Resources, who is a leader and innovator in sustainable food systems.
In addition, Jalbert took advantage of UConn’s co-op program and worked with both the Boston Beer Company, in new product development, and as a microbiology intern at the U.S. Department of Energy. Through exchange programs, he has learned about shellfish aquaculture in Melbourne, Australia, Manabi, Ecuador, as well as here in Connecticut.
Summer Accelerator: ‘I Must Have Learned 100 Things’
Part of Jalbert’s entrepreneurial journey included attending CCEI’s eight-week Summer Accelerator, which offers promising startups $15,000 in non-dilutive funding, mentorship, access to masterclasses and workshops, and pro-bono legal, accounting, marketing, product development, and banking services.
“Summer Accelerator is like a summer camp for startups,’’ Jalbert says. “It packs a lot into eight weeks. This summer we were testing how we can distribute our omega-3 product and learning the cost structures and economics of getting product to customers. I must have learned 100 things during Summer Accelerator, but the biggest thing was unit economics and cost structure of bringing the product to market.’’
With the oyster feed gaining traction, AccessFlora is focusing on educating people on the seafood nutrient. Jalbert just hired his first employee to work on business outreach. “We are in real talks with restaurants and agricultural experts,’’ he says.
AccessFlora also manages a food trailer, called Reef-to-Table, which caters weddings and other events. Although that isn’t the primary focus of the business, it is a terrific outlet for Jalbert.
“It’s a good way of having direct interactions with consumers. I enjoy it so much,’’ he says. “I have to be conscience of my time commitments, but if it could be my weekend hobby, I’d do it. The raw bar business is a ton of fun and already profitable.”
The Wolff New Venture Competition will be held on Tuesday (Oct. 13) at Pratt and Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford from 5 to 9 p.m. The event is free to attend and all are welcome. Pre-registration is required at https://luma.com/i2690pqa .
The Wolff New Venture Competition is supported by the generosity of the Wolff Family as well as wiggin(x), Fiondella, Milone & LaSaracina LLP, Sardilli Produce and Dairy Co., Prime Materials Recovery Inc., Big Bang, Baystate Financial, Webster Bank, Mark and Jamie Summers, Putnam Plastics, Eric Marziali, Bob and Linda Delisle, Dick and Carol Stewart and Event Resources.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.content_orig:
⛈️🌊 Track the storm, check your local risk and get more detailed timing from meteorologists in the CNN Weather app
If Isaias makes landfall as a hurricane, it will mark the first hurricane landfall anywhere in the United States in two years.
No hurricane has come ashore in the US since 2024’s Hurricane Milton . Milton slammed into Florida’s Gulf Coast as a Category 3 major hurricane on October 9, 2024.
Isaias is forecast to weaken, but still remain a formidable storm before landfall Friday night or very early Saturday morning. It could come ashore as a Category 1 or a lower-end Category 2 hurricane before quickly becoming a tropical storm after landfall.
Regardless of its strength, Isaias will be the fourth named storm to make landfall in the US this season. The three others have been short-lived tropical storms: Arthur impacted Texas on June 17; Bertha hit Louisiana on July 22; and Edouard made landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border on September 1.
All Mobile County and Baldwin County Public schools in Alabama will be closed on Friday as Hurricane Isaias is expected to impact the northern Gulf Coast this weekend.
“We do not like to do this, because it affects so many, but we have to take all factors into consideration and of course, the most important, the safety of our students and our staff,” Baldwin County Public Schools Superintendent Marty McRae said announcing the closure on Wednesday .
All of Baldwin County Public Schools’ afterschool and extracurricular activities scheduled for Friday and Saturday are also canceled.
“I cannot risk anyone’s safety,” Mobile County Public Schools Superintendent Chresal Threadgill said in his closure announcement . “The weather conditions currently remain extremely unpredictable.”
Isaias remains a Category 1 hurricane with sustained winds of 80 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center’s 7 a.m. CT update.
The hurricane has maintained its strength over the past few hours but is still set to strengthen today. It’s forecast to peak as a high-end Category 2 hurricane sometime Thursday night.
A Hurricane Hunter aircraft is currently flying into Isaias, so we’ll get a more precise measurement of its current strength soon.
At least 14 Florida Panhandle counties are closing public schools Friday, and many have closed Thursday, according to the state’s Department of Education.
Florida State University’s campus in Panama City is also closed.
The right side of a hurricane, relative to its forward motion, typically packs the most extreme conditions, and it’s all because of their counterclockwise rotation.
Wind speeds are amplified because the rotation pushes air in the same direction as the storm is moving. The area with the most extreme winds and intense storms sits just to the right of a hurricane’s eye, in the eye wall.
Because of boosted winds, tornadoes also occur more frequently on the right side. Faster winds increase areas of wind shear — a change in wind speed or direction with height — which tornadoes need to spin up.
Similarly, surge is also enhanced. As storms approach land, wind piles up and pushes seawater towards the coast on the right side of a hurricane. On the left side of a hurricane, wind does the opposite and can actually drain bays.
This will all be true for Isaias but may be even more so because it’s expected to become lopsided as it battles wind shear near the Gulf Coast. More thunderstorms and rain will likely be concentrated on the hurricane’s eastern half.
Isaias is guaranteed to knock out power and down trees where it makes landfall along the coast, but outages could extend further inland into parts of the Southeast.
Isaias will be moving fast and grow larger before it moves inland. Those are two of the factors that will fuel wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph that will spread northward into parts of central and northern Alabama, northern Georgia and northeast Mississippi on Saturday.
Those gusts are nowhere near as fierce as what the coast will see, but it could be enough to cause at least isolated to scattered power outages, particularly in Alabama.
As Tropical Storm Isaias heads towards the Gulf Coast, many residents began preparing days in advance.
Residents flocked to grocery stores and gas stations in Pensacola, Florida to stock up in preparation causing long lines at some locations.
As Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast, all eyes are on how it will impact one of the biggest games of the college football season.
The storm could make landfall Saturday, hours before No. 2 Georgia plays No. 6 Alabama in Tuscaloosa in a game that President Donald Trump is planning to attend.
While the storm could prompt other schools in the region to cancel games, change kickoff times, or even move games to other locations, Alabama said “there are no plans to alter the contest” in a statement Wednesday evening.
When asked whether the storm will change his travel plans to Alabama, Trump said, “We’ll have to see.”
Team officials offered few details on contingency plans if the storm were to intensify.
Even if the game goes on as planned, meteorologists predict players and spectators may feel some effects of the storm.
Heavy rain and gusty winds could make for a soggy, blustery Saturday evening in Tuscaloosa.
A faster-moving storm could allow conditions to improve before or during the game, but that’s not the most likely outcome right now. The timing will be key.
When Isaias rapidly intensified into a hurricane last night, it was undergoing a phenomenon that is becoming more common as the planet heats up.
Rapid intensification is when a storm’s sustained winds increase by at least 35 mph within 24 hours. The main ingredient a storm needs for this is ocean heat, which gives it the energy to build ferocious strength.
Global oceans absorb around 90% of the excess heat humans produce by burning oil, coal and gas — and they are warming at an alarming pace . The Gulf is no exception. Isaias is traveling over water that’s at record high temperatures for this time of year.
And because warmer air is able to hold more moisture, this could also supercharge the amount of rain Isaias is able to carry.
A 2024 study by the nonprofit research group Climate Central found climate change had boosted the intensity of most Atlantic hurricanes between 2019 and 2023.
Last year, four hurricanes underwent rapid intensification, including Category 5 Melissa , which tore across the Caribbean, killing more than 90 people.
Hurricane Isaias’s maximum sustained winds have increased to 80 mph, according to the 5 a.m. ET advisory from the National Hurricane Center.
Isaias forecast to strengthen into a Category 2 over the Gulf later today, then peak overnight at near Category 3, or major hurricane, intensity. How strong it gets will depend on how much Isaias can fend off increasing winds in the atmosphere that can rip storms apart.
Isaias is still expected to weaken some before landfall on Friday night, but that won’t reduce its danger. A life-threatening storm surge is expected at the coast and strong winds could down trees and knock out power well inland across parts of the South.
A state of emergency has been declared across Florida and Alabama.
Hurricane Isaias is due to make landfall late Friday night into Saturday as a strong Category two storm. A state of emergency has been declared across Florida and Alabama.
Isaias is now the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and has shattered the record for the latest first hurricane formation in the basin.
The previous record holders were 2002’s Hurricane Gustav and 2013’s Hurricane Humberto, both of which formed on September 11.
It’s also the first hurricane in the Atlantic basin in nearly a year: Hurricane Melissa was 2025’s final hurricane and it formed on October 25.
Gulf water is record warm for this time of year, helping to fuel the storm, but hostile atmospheric conditions near the coast are forecast to weaken Isaias a bit before it makes landfall Friday night or early Saturday

articles.title_zh: World Copper Announces Brassie Creek Claim Package Expanded by 1,473 Hectares to 3,335 Hectares
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Vancouver, British Columbia--(Newsfile Corp. - October 8, 2026) - World Copper Ltd. (TSXV: WCU) (OTCID: WCUFF) (FSE: 7LY2) (" World Copper " or the " Company ") is pleased to announce that the claim package for the Brassie Creek copper-gold project (the " Project ") in the Kamloops Mining District of south-central British Columbia has been expanded through the staking of additional contiguous mineral claims.
The newly staked claims add 1,473 hectares to the Project and increase the total optioned land position from 1,862 hectares to 3,335 hectares . The new ground lies immediately east of the Rattlesnake Creek area on the existing Brassie Creek claim package.
The additional claims were selected to cover prospective ground identified by earlier exploration immediately east of Rattlesnake Creek. Rattlesnake Creek is one of the principal target areas on the existing property. Previous operators have described it as a mineralized corridor associated with intrusive rocks and a historical induced polarization (IP) chargeability anomaly interpreted to remain open to the east.
The expanded package covers a larger contiguous block along the northern margin of the Guichon Creek Batholith, in the same regional copper belt that hosts Highland Valley Copper to the south. The Company interprets the new ground as extending coverage of the structural and exploration corridor already identified on the original Project claims.
About the Brassie Creek Project
The Brassie Creek Project is a porphyry-skarn copper and gold exploration prospect in the Kamloops Mining District, British Columbia. The Project has year-round road access from Highway 1 and the local forest service road network, and it sits in an established mining region with nearby infrastructure, services, and a skilled workforce based in Kamloops.
World Copper was granted the option to earn a 100% interest in the Project (the " Option ") by issuing 140,000 common shares on a post-consolidation basis, paying C$440,000, and spending C$750,000 over up to three years, subject to a 2% net smelter return royalty (NSR), of which 1% may be purchased for C$1.5 million. Because the 20-for-1 share consolidation effective July 17, 2026, fell within four months of the first share payment to the vendor, that tranche remains 100,000 post-consolidation shares. The unpaid tranches are adjusted to 10,000, 10,000, and 20,000 shares. The Company has no present ownership interest in the Project. If the Company does not meet the Option payment schedule, the Option will terminate and the Company will not retain any interest in the Project.

"World Food Day reminds us that everyday choices at the grocery store can help shape the future of food," said Raquel Isely, vice president of marketing at Natural Grocers. "We are proud to continue our support of The Cornucopia Institute and its important work to protect organic integrity for generations to come."

articles.title_orig: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.title_zh: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.content_orig:
by Brian White, Ashonti Ford
When most people think about dinosaur fossils, they may picture the wide-open landscapes of Montana, Wyoming or the Dakotas.
But some of the most significant fossil discoveries in the country are much closer to home — right here in Alabama.
Inside the Birmingham Mcwane Center, thousands of fossils are stored just feet away from visitors, offering a glimpse into an Alabama that existed long before the state — or even humans — were here.
Behind collection-room doors, row after row of cabinets hold bones, teeth and other remnants of life dating back more than half a billion years.
June Ebersole, director of collections at McWane Science Center, oversees about half a million specimens, including fossils found nowhere else in the world.
“A lot of people think you have to go out west to find fossils,” Ebersole said. “But what my research is showing is that Alabama, by far, is the number one state in the U.S. in terms of paleo-biodiversity.”
The collection spans an extraordinary stretch of time.
“We have fossils here that are over 500 million years old, to some that are just from the Ice Age, only 12,000 to 14,000 years old, and everything in between,” Ebersole said. “We have so many fossils here, I’m discovering new species all the time.”
Among the most remarkable specimens is one that helped change what scientists knew about dinosaurs in the eastern United States.
Ebersole opens a drawer containing the remains of Eotrachodon orientalis, a newly identified species of duck-billed dinosaur.
The fossils may look like a pile of bones to the untrained eye, but together they represent the most complete dinosaur ever found in the eastern half of the United States, with about 60% of its skeleton recovered.
And the discovery was made not in a remote western desert, but in Montgomery County.
“It’s from Montgomery County, right on the side of the creek, just outside the city limits,” Ebersole said. “This is the only one of this particular species in the world.”
The dinosaur is only part of Alabama’s prehistoric story.
The McWane collection also includes fossils of sharks, turtles and birds, along with a 315-million-year-old dragonfly wing discovered in Walker County.
Thousands of fossil shark teeth fill drawers inside the collection, including one massive collection from the time of the dinosaurs.
“It is literally — here’s 10,000 fossil goblin shark teeth,” Ebersole said. “It’s one of the biggest collections of these on the planet.”
Most visitors to the science center will see only a fraction of the collection.
But behind the scenes, scientists continue studying the specimens and making discoveries that help reconstruct the world that existed beneath Alabama millions of years ago.
Long before 250 years of American history, Alabama was already writing a story of its own — one measured not in centuries, but in hundreds of millions of years.
And today, pieces of that ancient story remain carefully preserved, waiting to reveal what Alabama looked like long before any of us arrived.

articles.title_orig: World Sight Day: HelpMeSee Calls for Greater Investment in Surgical Workforce to Address Global Cataract Blindness
articles.title_zh: World Sight Day: HelpMeSee Calls for Greater Investment in Surgical Workforce to Address Global Cataract Blindness
articles.content_orig:
JERSEY CITY, N.J., Oct. 8, 2026
JERSEY CITY, N.J. , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On World Sight Day , HelpMeSee is calling for greater investment in the skilled surgical workforce needed to address one of the world's most treatable causes of blindness.
It's estimated that 94 million adults age 50 and older live with vision impairment or blindness caused by untreated cataract, yet more than half of people who need cataract surgery globally do not have access to it. In the World Health Organization African Region, three in four people who need cataract surgery remain untreated.
Cataract can be treated surgically, but expanding access to treatment depends on having enough trained professionals with proficient surgical skills to provide quality care where patients need it most. Shortages and the unequal distribution of trained eye-care professionals remain significant barriers to cataract surgery, alongside cost, infrastructure and other health-system challenges.
"Expanding access to cataract treatment requires more than recognizing the scale of the problem. It requires sustained investment in the people and institutions that can provide quality surgical care. Building a skilled surgical workforce is essential to creating lasting cataract surgical capacity in communities where the need is greatest," says Dr. Nicoletta Fynn-Thompson, Chief Medical Officer at HelpMeSee.
The call comes at an important moment for global eye health. In September, the World Health Organization opened public consultation on a proposed Global Initiative to Eliminate Preventable Blindness and Vision Impairment, intended to accelerate progress toward the World Health Assembly target of increasing effective cataract surgery coverage by 30 percentage points by 2030.
World Sight Day also comes weeks before the Global Summit for Eye Health, where governments and global eye-health leaders will convene to advance action toward universal access to eye care.
Building Surgical Capacity Through Simulation
HelpMeSee works to address the surgical workforce challenge through competency-based, simulation-based cataract surgical training. Through partnerships with training institutions around the world, HelpMeSee supports the development of sustainable local surgical capacity and the effective transition of surgical skills into clinical practice.
The HelpMeSee training system combines high-fidelity virtual reality and realistic haptic feedback with structured curricula and instructor-led education. This approach enables trainees to repeatedly practice surgical skills, recognize and respond to complications, receive objective performance feedback and build competency in a simulated environment before transitioning those skills to live surgery.
Progress requires strong partnerships and sustained investment in the people, training and institutions needed to make quality cataract care accessible to communities around the world.
Advancing the Global Conversation
Beginning on World Sight Day, HelpMeSee is sponsoring a weeklong Healthcare Information For All (HIFA) Spotlight on Cataract Blindness, Surgical Quality, and the Value of Simulation-based Training , running October 8–14.
The international discussion will bring together health professionals, policymakers, researchers and others to examine the global burden of cataract, the availability and quality of surgery, the role of simulation-based training, and the policies and resources needed to expand access to quality cataract care.
"No single organization can close the global cataract treatment gap alone. Progress requires strong partnerships and sustained investment in the people, training and institutions that make quality cataract care possible," said Doug May, HelpMeSee President and CEO.
Addressing cataract blindness at the scale required will depend on coordinated action across governments, health systems, training institutions, NGOs, donors and local partners. Strengthening the surgical workforce and the institutions that support it must be a central part of that effort.
Support HelpMeSee on World Sight Day.
About HelpMeSee In a world where 100 million people are blind or visually impaired due to cataract, HelpMeSee, a not-for-profit under IRS 501(c)(3), has the global mission to eradicate cataract blindness by increasing the training of Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (MSICS). This high quality, very low-cost procedure delivers successful outcomes at a fraction of the cost of alternative procedures. The HelpMeSee MSICS training system features very high-fidelity, virtual reality simulation with realistic haptic feedback, sophisticated competency courseware, learning management systems, and electronic learning aids.
HelpMeSee was founded by Al and Jim Ueltschi, who imagined building the MSICS training system by incorporating many of the methods and techniques used successfully in commercial pilot training. As co-founder of Orbis International where he served as its chairman for 35 years. He founded FlightSafety International, the world's foremost aviation training company. Al Ueltschi was an icon in the aviation industry and was devoted to ending preventable blindness in the developing world. HelpMeSee trains high quality, very low-cost MSICS to ensure that all communities have access to sight restoring affordable treatment. With more than 40 simulators and 19 training centers worldwide, HelpMeSee partners with governments, universities and innovators to fight the global cataract blindness crisis. For more information, visit http://www.helpmesee.org .

articles.title_orig: Top Climate Scientists Set Out Five Steps to Help the World Prepare for Super El NiñO | Newswise
articles.title_zh: Top Climate Scientists Set Out Five Steps to Help the World Prepare for Super El NiñO | Newswise
articles.content_orig:
Newswise — Researchers have identified five key ways countries across the globe can be better prepared for the impending El Niño – and reduce its potentially devastating toll on human health.
The call to action , led by the University of Bristol and published in The Lancet , highlights how although it is widely-acknowledged El Niño exacerbates wide-ranging health risks posed by climate change, the additional threats presented remain largely unquantified. The researchers emphasise that as the El Niño cycle can be forecasted months in advance, preparatory measures should be put in place to mitigate the impact, especially in countries most vulnerable.
Study lead author Dr Ruby Lieber, Senior Research Associate in Climate Science at the University of Bristol, said: “We know the number of people affected by climate-related disasters is strongly influenced by the El Niño cycle, but there is little evidence available establishing how much of the health burden can be attributed to climate change and how much was driven by El Niño.
“Since the current El Niño pushes many regions into more extreme climates, there’s a pressing and unprecedented need to better understand, measure and pinpoint the different dangers for individual countries and places.”
The study recommends five important actions to gain this comprehensive risk overview, which holds the key to being able to tackle and minimise the likely consequences, including the spread of infectious diseases, malnutrition, and various heat-related conditions such as dehydration and heatstroke.
Dr Lieber said: “These steps will require greater collaboration between climate and health researchers and, equally fundamental, concerted action between research funders, the World Health Organization (WHO), the wider UN system, the World Bank, and non-governmental organisations.
“Partnership working is imperative and such global entities need to urgently call on advances in attribution science to more accurately recognise and assess how much of the repercussions are the result of human-induced climate change and how much are a result of El Niño. By isolating the El Niño-related impacts, we can generate much more targeted and event-specific actions.”
A significant El Niño, which describes the warming of sea surface temperature, is likely to occur towards the end of this year with some forecasts predicting the strongest event on record. The direct effects of El Niño will be felt across the globe and may heighten instances of extreme weather in regions such as India, East Asia, South America, parts of Africa and the West Pacific.
Co-author Dann Mitchell, Shanta Professorial Chair in Planetary Health at the University of Bristol, added: “It’s clear that we cannot afford to ignore this emerging threat, which poses potentially devastating but predictable risks to communities around the world.
“Climate and health researchers must unite, with the full backing of national and international agencies, to create a much more advanced evidence base. This will enable us to ramp up global resilience and implement adaptation strategies to mitigate the many deeply concerning health implications, particularly for countries more acutely exposed.”

articles.content_orig:
COLUMBIA, Md., Oct. 8, 2026
Powered by UL Research Institutes, the Communities of Practice offer a sustained mechanism to share knowledge, align on emerging risks, and rapidly translate research across borders
COLUMBIA, Md. , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Following the biennial gathering of the world's fire leaders at the World Fire Congress, UL Research Institutes' Fire Safety Research Institute is powering the ongoing Communities of Practice (CoPs) to advance solutions for the most pressing global fire safety issues. The structured and sustained CoPs will accelerate progress through monthly thematic sessions, shared governance, robust information distribution and direct integration of frontline research.
"The inaugural World Fire Congress and Communities of Practice in 2024 established the foundation for sustained and collaborative knowledge exchange, and ULRI is honored to build on that foundation," said Dr. Lori Moore-Merrell, World Fire Congress founder and chief fire safety strategist for the Fire Safety Research Institute. "Drawing on more than a century of fire research and leadership, ULRI is bringing its scientific rigor into the global conversation, ensuring the dialogue is grounded in evidence over anecdote."
The World Fire Congress CoPs offer the fire service a mechanism to share knowledge, align on emerging risks and translate research and training into practice across borders. Through ULRI, members gain access to a trusted international network, curated best practices and direct engagement with leading researchers and their work on areas including lithium-ion battery safety, EV fire risk, climate adaptation and evidence-based tactical decision-making. Each CoP will be equipped with the necessary infrastructure to collaborate across nations and will be grounded with an Anchor Organization to bring established expertise and leadership to each Community.
The 2026 - 2028 CoPs, along with their Anchor Organizations, include:
In addition to Moore-Merrell, CoPs leadership includes Mark Hardingham, CoPs Ambassador. With a career spanning four decades from UK firefighter to Chief Fire Officer to former chair of the UK National Fire Chiefs Council.
Diane Haithcock serves as CoPs Administrator. Haithcock is Director, Program Manager for UL Standards & Engagement (ULSE) where she oversees ULSE Technical Committee chairs and project managers across the U.S. and Canada for standards related to life safety products, physical security, building materials, and wildland-urban interface. In collaboration with ULRI's Fire Safety Research Institute, ULSE supports monthly meetings, research analysis, and reports for CoPs members.
The World Fire Congress is a biennial global forum bringing together fire and emergency service leaders, government representatives, researchers and partners to strengthen international cooperation, share knowledge and support evidence-informed discussion on fire and life safety challenges facing communities worldwide. The inaugural World Fire Congress was held in Washington D.C. in 2024. The National Fire Chiefs Council hosted the second World Fire Congress in London, September 8-9, 2026, with representatives from more than 60 nations attending.
The World Fire Congress is led by an international steering committee, including the host nation, and supported by the Metropolitan Fire Chiefs Association (Metro Chiefs) as its Secretariat. Metro Chiefs is a section of the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) and the International Association of Fire Chiefs (IAFC). The Secretariat provides continuity between Congresses, supports host nations and helps sustain international collaboration between events.
The next World Fire Congress will be hosted by Dubai Civil Defence in the United Arab Emirates in February 2028.
For more information visit WFCCOP.fsri.org .
About Fire Safety Research Institute UL Research Institutes' Fire Safety Research Institute advances fire science and fire safety knowledge to reduce risk, save lives, and protect property. We conduct rigorous research, outreach, and education in collaboration with the fire service, fire safety professionals, policymakers, communities, and an international network of partners. Together, we develop tools, resources, and strategies that improve fire safety outcomes worldwide. To learn more, visit fsri.org . Follow Fire Safety Research Institute on Instagram , Facebook , and LinkedIn .
About UL Standards & Engagement UL Standards & Engagement is a nonprofit organization that translates safety science into action through standards development, partnerships, and advocacy. Since 1903, we have developed nearly 1,700 standards and guidance documents for products ranging from fire doors to autonomous vehicles. ULSE enables innovation and grows trust by convening experts and informing policymakers and regulators as we work toward a safer, more secure and sustainable future. Visit ULSE.org for more information.
About UL Research Institutes UL Research Institutes is a nonprofit research organization dedicated to advancing public safety through scientific discovery. Since 1894, our research has advanced our mission toward a safer, more secure and sustainable future. Focused on global risks from fire mitigation and air quality to safe energy storage and digital privacy, we conduct rigorous independent research, analyze safety data and partner with experts to uncover and act on existing and emerging risks to human safety. Discover more at UL.org .
About the World Fire Congress The World Fire Congress is a biennial global forum focused on strengthening international cooperation, knowledge sharing, and evidence-informed dialogue on fire and life safety challenges facing communities worldwide. Guided by its founding principles, the Congress brings together fire and emergency service leaders, researchers, and partners to advance collaboration on firefighter health and safety, wildfires, structural fires, emerging technologies, prevention, response, recovery, and resilience.
