articles.title_orig: What’s the Matter With France?
articles.title_zh: What’s the Matter With France?
articles.content_orig:
France’s unprecedented wave of student protests has laid bare the country’s growing financial pressures, which will only become more difficult to tackle as Europe’s second-largest economy tries to rein in a ballooning budget deficit.
The country’s finances are in a precarious state. Public debt was more than $4 trillion in June, exceeding the size of the economy, according to the country’s statistics agency . The cost of servicing that debt has climbed by billions of dollars on last year, as bond yields spike .
At the same time, demands on the public purse are rising: Pension costs have climbed because of an aging population while the government looks to spend more on defense.
High school students, meanwhile, have called for a fix to staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure.
Solutions to France’s financial troubles have led to social unrest in the past. Efforts to raise the retirement age sparked widespread protests in 2023 .
French school protests grow as workers join students
Last week, the French government proposed deep spending cuts and tax hikes aimed at narrowing the budget deficit, but bond buyers are concerned that fiscal measures may be watered down by lawmakers ahead of presidential elections next year, said Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at consultancy Capital Economics.
The election could see President Emmanuel Macron ousted by either a far-right or far-left successor, raising questions over the country’s commitment to fiscal discipline. While Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally recently proposed substantial spending cuts meant to stabilize the public finances, her party also remains committed to costly tax reductions, Kenningham said.
“Investors will also be concerned about greater fiscal populism after the elections,” he wrote in a note last week. “There is a big risk that spreads rise a lot further, either before or after next year’s elections.”
Worries about a potential debt crisis in France boiled over last week, leading to a selloff in French bonds and a sharp rise in yields.
The spread between French and German bond yields expanded to its widest level since 2012. That difference in yields means investors are demanding much higher returns to hold debt from France compared with Germany, which is deemed a safer alternative.
The French bond rout has sparked fears of spillovers to other high-yield European debt markets, with some analysts drawing parallels with the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s .
Global bond sell-off deepens, sending borrowing costs higher around the world
Given France’s size and systemic importance, “the potential for contagion into other countries and the Eurozone at large is very large and could potentially cause a serious crisis for the entire region,” Angel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, an advisory firm, told CNN.
These worries in large part pushed the euro to its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025 on Monday. The currency, shared by 21 countries in the European Union, is worth around $1.12, having briefly dipped below that level.
The latest ructions in markets could weigh on a fragile economic recovery in Europe, bolstered by investment into artificial intelligence, stronger demand for European exports and higher defense spending in Germany.
Recent survey data showed that activity in manufacturing and services in the euro area increased at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years last month.
“(Economic) growth is staging a comeback and Europe has shown surprising resilience,” economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a late September note.
Fall of yet another premier will make it hard for France to fix its finances. What’s behind its debt problem?
High bond yields are a clear risk to that growth, however.
If governments don’t cut spending , “interest rates will continue to go up,” Carsten Brzeski, head of macroeconomics at Dutch bank ING told CNN.
Higher bond yields push up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy, making home and car purchases more expensive and driving down investment. They also make it more expensive for governments to borrow money and force a certain degree of austerity to stop yields from rising further.
Yields on French, German and UK government bonds have broken multi-year records in recent weeks as concerns mount about the sustainability of public debt loads.
Europe’s public finances pose “serious risks to eurozone financial markets and to the economy,” Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics, told CNN.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV Urges Rediscovery of Beauty in a Technology-Driven World
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV Urges Rediscovery of Beauty in a Technology-Driven World
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday urged patrons of the Vatican Museums to rediscover beauty in an era dominated by technology.
The pontiff held a private audience on Oct. 7 at the Vatican with the Louisiana chapter of the patrons during their pilgrimage to Rome. The Patrons of the Arts in the Vatican Museums, founded in 1983, is an international group of benefactors who fund the conservation and restoration of the Vatican’s art collections.
Leo, in his remarks , thanked them for their collaboration and support for the Vatican Museums and invited them to create spaces of beauty in a world where technology is often preferred.
“In an age dominated by technology, in which efficiency and profit often take precedence, it is so important that we continue to cultivate a spirit of contemplation and allow time and space for beauty,” Leo said.
He also added that fostering this attitude would “greatly help humanity, especially young people, not only to discover the ability of art to uplift and reveal the depths of the human spirit.”
“Ultimately,” Leo added, “contemplation presents a marvelous opportunity to encounter the God who is beauty, whom St. Augustine described as ever-ancient and ever-new.”
Leo’s remarks followed his address during a private audience with artists on Oct. 2 in which he explained the difference between authentic art and art created by artificial intelligence (AI).
“There is an ontological difference — even before an aesthetic one — between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of the human, whereas ‘authentic culture and art preserve this spark,’” Leo said, quoting from his encyclical on AI, Magnifica Humanitas .

articles.title_orig: A Vail mountaineer is vying to be the first American woman to scale the world's tallest volcanoes
articles.title_zh: A Vail mountaineer is vying to be the first American woman to scale the world's tallest volcanoes
articles.content_orig:
In August 2024, Vail’s Nicole Otake climbed Papua New Guinea’s Mount Giluwe, the highest volcano in Oceania.
Getting there required the kind of logistics that adventurous travelers love: “A guy picked us up at the airport, then handed us off to another guy and his son who connected us to someone else,” Otake said.
This story first appeared in The Outsider , the premium outdoor newsletter by Jason Blevins. In it, he covers the industry from the inside out, plus the fun side of being outdoors in our beautiful state.
Eventually, Otake and her climbing partner were led to a few men on the side of a road in Papua New Guinea’s Western Highlands where they all began a two-day trek toward the mountain. The men were barefoot and carried handmade spears.
Giluwe rises 14,327 feet — not especially high by mountaineering standards — but the climb was muddy, wet and remote. Along the way, Otake saw enormous prehistoric-looking birds running through the highlands.
“It was like being back in time,” Otake said. “It was super remote and super cool.”
It was also the fourth stop on a checklist: climbing the Seven Volcanic Summits, the highest volcanoes on each continent.
Otake, 32, has so far summited six of the seven. All that remains is Mount Sidley in Antarctica, the most remote of the seven and by far the most expensive to reach. If Otake gets there, she will become the first American woman to complete the Seven Volcanic Summits.
Otake started climbing mountains because she liked the idea of a challenge she could quantify. She is analytical and she likes spreadsheets and lists. The Seven Volcanic Summits gave her all three — along with a reason to start learning how to climb increasingly big and remote mountains.
Then, the mountains started leading her somewhere she hadn’t expected. From one summit, she would look across a valley and see another peak — one that wasn’t on any list, wasn’t particularly well known and, in some cases, was rarely climbed.
“Now there are so many mountains that aren’t on any of these lists that are so much higher on my list,” she said.
That shift — from checking off summits to seeking out remote mountains for their own sake — has also changed the way Otake thinks about mountaineering. She has learned how expensive and complicated mountaineering can be, and how much knowledge it takes to get into the mountains without paying someone else to handle everything. She has also learned that the sport is still overwhelmingly male and that many aspiring climbers, particularly women, lack the mentorship and resources she wished she had.
So this year, after losing the remote leadership job that had helped finance her climbing, Otake started Ash to Altitude, a small logistics company designed to help people plan their own expeditions — without the luxury price tag.
“I really believe people need access to these mountains,” she said.
Otake’s first big mountain — also one of the Seven Volcanic Summits — was Kilimanjaro, which she climbed in March 2023 in less than three days.
She had always been interested in volcanoes. Her father was born in Hawaii before it became a state , and because of that Otake grew up with a connection to the islands and the volcanoes that shape them. As she learned more about volcanoes around the world, she came across the Seven Volcanic Summits.
Learning that no American woman had completed the seven gave her new motivation.
“Someone will always be stronger or faster,” Otake said. “But you can’t take away the first of something.”
At first, the goal was simply to complete the list. But as Otake and her husband, Rocco, planned and executed the expeditions, they got hooked on going higher and farther. Rocco was also interested in climbing the traditional Seven Summits, the highest mountain on each continent, and the two began taking on bigger objectives together. In the process, Otake became the person handling the logistics.
“It lets my spreadsheet brain be happy,” she said.
The more mountains they climbed — like Denali and Mount Elbrus and Pico de Orizaba — the more the list became a gateway into alpine climbing. Each expedition taught them something about planning, logistics and what they were capable of taking on next. Ticking boxes became less and less important.
“Starting with a list has given us the skills and tools to become better mountaineers,” Otake said. “It was a good way to start because I wasn’t sure of anything else. But now there are so many mountains that aren’t on any of these lists that are so much more intriguing.”
Like Alpamayo in Peru, which she calls the most beautiful mountain in the world.
Even that experience, Otake said, made her want to look beyond the mountain she was climbing.
“But as we’re climbing that, it’s like, look across the valley and there’s Artesonraju , which is even more beautiful,” she said. “So now we’re going back next June.”
That curiosity has pushed Otake toward increasingly remote and self-supported objectives. She and Rocco have learned how to arrange their own transportation, permits, lodging, food and acclimatization rather than simply signing up for a commercial expedition and showing up at the trailhead.
Otake likes that part almost as much as the climbing.
She and Rocco live full time in a solar-powered van, spending much of the winter in the Vail Valley and leaving in the summer to climb. The van is minimalist: Otake says she owns one dress and one pair of heels, which both live crammed into a wheel well, while the couple’s climbing and skiing gear occupies the remaining space.
The setup suits a life organized around mountains. When she’s not climbing, Otake is usually planning the next climb — researching routes, comparing costs, figuring out transportation and finding people on the ground who can help them navigate places they have never been.
The process has given Otake a crash course in the barriers to mountaineering — not just the physical ones, but the financial and logistical ones, too. She has learned how much it costs to get to these places, how difficult it can be to know whom to trust and how much easier the process becomes if someone else has already figured it out.
The more time she spent in the mountains, the more Otake also noticed how difficult it can be for someone else to get started. Mountaineering is expensive. There is the gear, the international travel, the time required for training and acclimatization, and, for many mountains, thousands of dollars paid to an expedition company to arrange the logistics and guide the climb.
Otake had been fortunate. For four and a half years, she worked in leadership at Act Blue, a digital fundraising platform that builds open-access software for Democratic campaigns, progressive organizations, and 501(c)(3) organizations. The remote role allowed her to take extended time away for climbing. She bought her van and most of her equipment and learned how to organize increasingly complicated expeditions herself. “I was really lucky,” she said.
So, when Otake lost that job in May of 2025, she decided to try her hand at professionalizing something she already knew how to do.
In February, she started Ash to Altitude, a small expedition-planning company that helps climbers arrange their own trips. The idea is to work directly with local operators and strip away the overhead of a fully packaged expedition. Because Otake has already done so many expeditions herself, she knows how much they can cost — versus how much is often charged. She said she has seen companies charge about $7,000 for an Elbrus expedition that she can organize for roughly $3,000, including flights and a visa.
“It drives me crazy to see people exploit other people, especially to go to parts of the world where they can’t promote local pricing,” she says.
The business is still small — so far, many of her clients have come through friends and Instagram — but the idea extends beyond saving money. Otake wants to make the information and experience she has accumulat

articles.title_orig: Chinese militia boat spotted for first time off Taiwan's Pacific coast
articles.title_zh: Chinese militia boat spotted for first time off Taiwan's Pacific coast
articles.content_orig:
A vessel, which APEX Aviation says is Chinese fishing boat Minfudingyu 07902 is seen off Taiwan's east coast in mid-August 2026 | Photo: APEX Aviation/Handout via REUTERS
A militia craft from China was recorded with two other ships off Taiwan's Pacific coast in August, according to Reuters , the first such sighting. The ship, identified in an Apex Aviation report seen by Reuters as the Minfudingyu 07902, is a fishing boat that serves as a militia vessel. It was sailing along with a coast guard cutter and a research ship.
China has raised east-coast patrols since June and claims the island. Officials in Taiwan call this blockade practice mixing military, paramilitary and civilian assets. Eastern waters are vital for wartime allied supplies.
Taiwanese defense officials told Reuters that China was "using law enforcement and scientific research as cover for harassment, seeking to expand their scope of operations during a non-conflict scenario to create an illusion of de facto jurisdiction." They said the steps undermine order and maritime rights. China's Taiwan Affairs Office and Ministry of National Defense did not respond.
The maritime militia dates to the 1950s and appears more often in the South China Sea. Analysts say it lets Beijing press claims while looking civilian. Two senior Taiwan officials confirmed the Minfudingyu, cutter 2502 and Xiang Yang Hong 03 were near Taiwan in mid-August. One official said the boat, in the People's Liberation Army maritime militia fleet, was operating "in coordination with Chinese coast guard maritime harassment drills." "The purpose of militia boats is to conduct substantive harassment," the official said. The other official said the three craft were operating "in an area not commonly used by Chinese vessels" and had been "designated for heightened monitoring."
An Apex plane found a Chinese group more than 30 nautical miles (34.5 miles) off Hualien, and the firm withheld the date over counter-reconnaissance concerns. Apex says the flights are independent yet fit the government's "whole of society resilience" initiative.
Honor Hung of Apex said warships, coast guard vessels, research ships and some civilian craft keep overlapping, "creating pressure in the waters surrounding Taiwan." The three ships sat across 10 nautical miles (11.5 miles). A light plane with a US-made radar can detect surface objects as small as 900 square centimeters (140 square inches), Reuters reported.

articles.title_orig: Gruesome injuries throw spotlight on France’s policing of high school protests
articles.title_zh: Gruesome injuries throw spotlight on France’s policing of high school protests
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — The police tear gas grenade shattered the 14-year-old’s jaw and many of his teeth. The officer who fired it was taken into custody a week later and charged with violent mutilation, punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Following surgery, the boy cannot speak and can only eat with a straw, his mother says.
Other adolescents have also suffered life-changing injuries blamed on police weaponry during nationwide protests by high school students demanding more funding for run-down schools. In the former mining town of Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. In Tours, in the wine-making Loire region, the prosecutor there says a police riot-control round is suspected in the partial blinding of a 16-year-old.
Beyond physical wounds, the massive use of police arrests and tactics that government critics and human rights campaigners allege have been unnecessarily violent is giving a generation of French schoolchildren — and soon-to-be voters — a real-life education about state power and their rights as citizens, and how the two sometimes clash.
“It politicizes you at an incredible speed,” said Alexis Baudelin, a Paris attorney for more than a dozen youngsters taken into custody.
“For many of them — for all of them — this was one of the first times that they’d taken part in a demonstration, coming together in a public space to voice demands they considered legitimate.”
Police have swept up thousands of young people
According to the Interior Ministry, police have made more than 6,600 arrests — mostly of people under 18 — since protests began snowballing last week, including 488 people detained during nationwide demonstrations Tuesday. The movement demanding increased funds and more replacement teachers for schools started in a Paris-region high school in mid-September.
Lawyers and researchers who study French policing caution that the muscular response could spawn disillusioned young adults soured on the Republic and its promises of “ Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. “Police have been less forgiving with teenage protesters than they previously were when farmers, a powerful lobby in France, doused government buildings with manure, blocked roads and set fires.
Baudelin, the lawyer, said his young clients have had a crash course in “unrestrained violence from the police.”
“Being locked up for hours and hours with nothing, in cells that are for the most part extremely unsanitary, in police stations that smell terrible, where you can’t sleep, with police officers telling you that if you don’t talk, if you don’t tell the truth, threatening you, telling you that your life is going to be ruined,” he said.
“It’s an experience that can be deeply traumatic and is completely out of proportion.”
Amid a growing outcry, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced Wednesday that the model of stun grenade suspected of mutilating the teenager in Lens will no longer be used against high schoolers, in light, he said, of a “strong possibility” that such a weapon was involved in ripping off the pupil’s hand.
“We need to understand exactly what happened,” Nunez said.
Still, he has also defended police actions as proportionate in “almost all cases.” He says police have been obliged to intervene when protests led to rioting, vandalism and other violence, and have done so mindful that they’re largely dealing with children.
“You don’t handle a high schoolers’ movement in the same way as one by adults,” the minister said to broadcaster RTL.
In the case of the 14-year-old with a smashed jaw and teeth, the officer who fired his grenade launcher directly at him during a protest in Saint-Ouen l’Aumone, northwest of Paris, said during questioning in custody that he acted in “a fraction of a second” to protect a female colleague who’d exchanged blows with the boy, according to a statement from the prosecutor’s office leading the investigation.
It described the officer’s actions as disproportionate, resulting in a preliminary charge against him of violence by a public official causing mutilation or permanent disability. Suspended from duty and barred from carrying a gun, he is the first officer facing potential prosecution in 18 investigations opened so far into suspected police misconduct during the protests.
The boy, Eden, sent his mother a video from outside his school, showing police and some protesters, just moments before the officer shot him with the gas grenade, she said, speaking to The Associated Press and other media on condition that she not be identified to preserve the anonymity of her child.
But when she then called him, it was one of his classmates who answered, screaming that her son had been hit in the face and was on the ground, bleeding with his jaw and top teeth broken and bottom teeth “completely ripped out,” she said.
“It’s shameful, it’s appalling, it’s violent, it’s disgusting, it’s despicable — I could give you a whole list of words,” she said. “They are dealing with children. And children demanding what? Simply better conditions in which to study.”
In the crowds that demonstrated in Paris on Tuesday, marching boisterously from one city square to another, AP found three Paris-region teenagers who said they were arrested, handcuffed, searched, held in custody but then released with no criminal charges last week.
Samy and Warkya, both 17, said they were detained together with another friend. They believe that police picked on them because of their color. Warkya and the other friend are Black and Samy described himself as Arab. French officials have repeatedly denied that there is racism in the police ranks. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said in parliament this week that such accusations are “lies.”
Samy said the officers who stopped them said, “’You, you and you, you’re coming with us.’” There was no apparent motive, because “we weren’t wearing hoodies, we had nothing on us, our faces were visible,” he said.
“Here in France, they don’t listen to us. They would rather send in the police than listen to us and put measures in place to improve our daily lives,” he said.
Warkya said her first experience of police custody only reinforced her determination to protest but also taught her to run when officers appear.
“The police are more powerful than us,” she said. “There’s nothing we can do.”

articles.title_orig: Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say
articles.title_zh: Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say
articles.content_orig:
A landmark report reveals that the world must change the way it produces food to avoid a biodiversity collapse
Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.
The World Wildlife Fund ( WWF ) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.
Nature loss is no longer just an environmental challenge but a direct threat to the global economy, the report says, noting that about half of global GDP – roughly $58tn (£44tn) in 2023 – depends on nature and its ecosystem services. The authors write that species collapse now poses an “existential threat to economic stability, geopolitical security and human wellbeing”.
Animal populations were found to be falling most sharply in tropical, biodiversity-rich regions, while trends in northern temperate parts of the world appeared much gentler.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, land and freshwater wildlife populations fell by an average of 95% between 1970 and 2022, while the equivalent declines were 80% in Africa and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.
Freshwater wildlife suffered the sharpest losses across the world’s ecosystems, with monitored populations in rivers and lakes down by an average of 85%, compared with 69% for land species and 59% for marine species.
Tanya Steele, the chief executive of WWF UK, said: “Nature loss is not just a crisis for wildlife. It’s already sending us the bill through growing risks to our food security, water supplies, economy and resilience to climate shocks.
“We stand at a fork in the road: either we continue paying the rising price of nature loss, or we invest in nature’s recovery and a future where people and wildlife can thrive together.”
But despite the pattern of global biodiversity decline, wild tigers, green sea turtles and bluefin tuna are recovering, the report said, showing that “it is still possible to reverse the global loss of nature when action is taken”.
In 2010, about 3,200 wild tigers remained globally and the species was sliding toward extinction. After sustained and targeted conservation interventions, the population has grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%.
Becci May, WWF UK’s tiger lead, said the remarkable comeback of wild tigers demonstrated the “science of hope” and proved that when climate and ecological action was taken, change was possible.
The report said Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna populations, which were collapsing after decades of overfishing, had now recovered to the point where neither was now considered threatened.
Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever downlisted from endangered to “least concern” on the IUCN red list, reflecting 50 years of coordinated conservation work across about 80 countries.
Dr Mike Barrett, the chief scientific adviser for WWF UK and a co-author of the report, said: “These are examples that show that nature can recover even when pushed right to the brink, and they provide us with inspiration. It’s also very clear that conservation alone cannot tackle the scale of threats facing nature.”
He said nature would have no chance of recovery if “negative tipping points ” – self-reinforcing, irreversible ecological changes that accelerate climate crisis – were passed. “The systems which drive nature’s loss have to be transformed. And that’s energy, food and finance,” he said.
“Our report shows that we’ve already passed the tipping point in the energy sector with the take-up of renewable energy . That transition is now unstoppable. It’s not happening fast enough, but it is unstoppable.”
Humanity must likewise adapt the way it produces food, he said. “Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and therefore the loss of biodiversity. It’s also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and so helps drive climate change, so you have that feedback.”
Dr Steve Smith, a research fellow from the University of Exeter and a co-author of the report, said: “The biggest prize for nature recovery would be a sustainable and healthy food system, but it’s currently the farthest away from positively tipping. For example, agricultural expansion drives almost 90% of deforestation worldwide.”
Positive tipping points are thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.

articles.title_orig: UNESCO and Partners Mark World Teachers’ Day in Sudan, Putting
articles.title_zh: UNESCO and Partners Mark World Teachers’ Day in Sudan, Putting
articles.content_orig:
On World Teachers’ Day 2026, UNESCO, in partnership with the Ministry of Education, Sudanese National Commission for Education, Science and Culture (NATCOM), teachers, students and education stakeholders in Khartoum, came together to recognise and reaffirm a shared priority: teachers must be at the heart of Sudan’s education recovery.
“We see your sacrifice. We recognize your value. And we stand with you. Supporting teachers means supporting Sudan’s future.” - Mr. Junaid Sorosh-Wali, Head of Office and UNESCO Representative to Sudan
This year’s World Teachers’ Day was celebrated globally under the theme “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures.”
The commemoration marks 60 years since the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers, a landmark international instrument that established principles concerning teachers’ rights and responsibilities, professional preparation, employment and working conditions.
In Sudan, these principles carry particular significance today.
Reflecting the realities facing the country’s education system, the national celebration adopted the message “Together with Sudan’s Teachers: Sustaining Education and Strengthening the Teaching Profession.”
It recognises teachers who have continued to support learners despite conflict, displacement, disrupted schooling and difficult working conditions, while drawing attention to what will be needed for the future: stronger professional development, adequate support and greater investment in the people on whom education ultimately depends.
The celebration brought together representatives of the Ministry of Education, NATCOM, teachers, students and other education stakeholders. It also marked the beginning of further World Teachers’ Day activities in schools across Khartoum, bringing recognition of teachers closer to the communities where they work every day.
For Dr. Muawia Gashi, Director-General of the National Centre for Teacher Training , strengthening the profession is inseparable from improving education itself.
“Teachers are behind every profession and are fundamental to the quality of the entire education system. Investing in their training, professional development and empowerment is essential to improving learning quality.”
UNESCO Sudan continues to work with national education authorities and partners to strengthen the resilience of the education system and support teachers through capacity development in education in emergencies, technical education, literacy and accelerated learning programmes, inclusive education for learners with disabilities, education planning and coordination, as well as broader efforts to improve the quality of teaching and learning.
This investment is particularly important as Sudan works to sustain education during the crisis while preparing for longer-term recovery. Supporting teachers with the skills, professional opportunities and conditions they need is fundamental to building an education system that can respond to disruption while remaining inclusive and focused on quality learning.
In February 2026, UNESCO Sudan, in partnership with the National Center for Teacher Training, brought together 30 teacher-training experts from across Sudan’s states to support the adaptation and accreditation of teacher-training packages for education in emergencies. The initiative sought to strengthen the quality and consistency of teacher training, improve coordination between national and state-level structures, and equip teachers with approaches better suited to crisis-affected learning environments.
This work forms part of broader efforts to support the implementation of Sudan’s Transitional Education Plan 2025–2027 , which provides a framework for restoring access to education, strengthening system resilience and responding to the needs of learners and education personnel affected by the crisis.
Some of the most meaningful voices of the day came from the students themselves.
Students from Sulieman Bushara School brought the celebration to life through two choral performances dedicated to their teachers. Through song, they expressed appreciation for the people who teach and guide them, while sharing messages of hope as students and teachers begin a new school year.
Their participation brought the purpose of World Teachers’ Day back to where the relationship between teaching and learning is experienced every day: between teachers and their students.
For UNESCO, celebrating teachers must go beyond recognition. It also means sustained attention to their professional development, status, well-being and working conditions.
As Sudan works to keep learning going today and rebuild its education system for tomorrow, strengthening the teaching profession will be essential to creating a system that is more resilient, inclusive and capable of delivering quality education for every learner.
This World Teachers’ Day, the message from Khartoum was clear: standing with Sudan’s teachers is an investment in the learners they serve and in the country’s future.

articles.title_orig: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it | CNN Business
articles.title_zh: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it | CNN Business
articles.content_orig:
The global energy system is already being pushed to the brink. A hurricane barreling down on America’s refining nerve center is the last thing that’s needed.
Isaias, the Atlantic season’s first hurricane , is arriving at a time when there is almost no margin for error.
US refineries, mostly located along the Gulf Coast, are running as hard as they can to offset war-driven outages overseas. Fuel inventories that act as shock absorbers have already been tapped. And America’s emergency oil stockpile is at the lowest level since 1982.
Hurricane Isaias “could be a gigantic event. It’s the worst time something like this could happen in 25 years,” said Robert Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho Securities.
The actual impact of Isaias will depend on the storm’s path and intensity.
Current forecasts call for the storm to hit east of New Orleans, a major refining hub, which should spare vital energy infrastructure from the storm’s worst.
Still, major oil producers including Shell, Chevron and BP have evacuated non-essential personnel from oil platforms in the Gulf and curtailed production .
As of midday Wednesday, about 512,000 barrels per day of Gulf of Mexico oil production had been shut in, according to the federal agency Marine Minerals Administration.
That amounts to about 25% of the region’s production. And about 16% of current natural gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has been sidelined.
The risk is that the storm’s damage could squeeze supply chains even more, further raising historically high prices.
The Iran war, combined with Ukrainian drone attacks in Russia and export restrictions in China, have catapulted diesel prices to all-time highs. Gasoline was more than $4.40 per gallon last week and has never been this expensive at this time of year.
About 2.7 million barrels per day, or 14%, of America’s refining capacity, lie within or near the projected of the path of the storm, according to Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
Lipow said he expects at least some refineries in the New Orleans/Baton Rouge and Mississippi/Alabama regions will have to slow down how much oil they turn into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
Tankers delivering oil to refineries and loading fuel out of refineries could get delayed as well. This would particularly impact Florida because the state relies on shipments of fuel from the Gulf Coast.
“There is no slack in the system to make up for lost refinery capacity. Lost production will have to come out of already low commercial inventories,” Lipow wrote in an email.
Those commercial inventories have been whittled away.
Gasoline stockpiles recently fell to their lowest seasonal record since 2012, according to federal data.
Distillate inventories, which include mostly diesel, are at their lowest level for early October since tracking started in the early 1980s.
Not only that, but the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has been aggressively drained to ease the energy shock. The SPR now holds about 283 million barrels of crude, the least since 1982 when the emergency reserve was being filled during the Reagan administration.
Refineries in the Middle East have been damaged by the Iran war, or have struggled to get shipments out to the rest of the world. Refineries in Russia have been destroyed or damaged by drone attacks. And China, seeking to avoid fuel shortages, has restricted its exports.
US refineries, operating at about 95% of their capacity, are one of the remaining key sources for the global fuel supply.
“It would be a disaster if US refining capacity has to come off the market. It would basically force a diesel export ban,” said Yawger, the Mizuho executive, who added that he is not in favor of restricting US diesel exports .
Much depends on the intensity of the storm, including the severity of flooding and wind damage. Isaias could peak as a Category 2 storm with 110 mph winds by early Friday, but is expected to weaken somewhat before landfall.
Even with a Category 1 hurricane, it can take a week to return refining operations to normal.

articles.title_orig: What vaccines doctors say you may need for respiratory virus season - ABC News
articles.title_zh: What vaccines doctors say you may need for respiratory virus season - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Doctors discuss COVID, flu and RSV vaccines recommended this year.
As the weather turns colder, it also means respiratory virus season is upon the United States.
In its annual outlook report , the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it expects the 2026-27 respiratory virus season to have a similar number of peak hospitalizations from influenza, COVID-19 and RSV compared to last season.
Public health specialists told ABC News the best way for people to protect themselves against these viruses is to get vaccinated.
The CDC currently recommends that people aged 6 months and older receive an annual flu vaccine.
The seasonal flu vaccine protects against three viruses predicted to circulate during flu season: Type A (H1N1) virus, Type A(H3N2) virus, and Type B/Victoria virus
There are several flu vaccines available this season, with recommendations varying by age and medical history.
"Obviously, we target high-risk groups, so those would be older adults, so over the age of 50, people with chronic medical conditions, individuals who are immunocompromised, individuals that have obesity, or persons who are pregnant or wanting to get pregnant, and healthcare personnel," Dr. Michael Angarone, director of the Infectious Disease Fellowship Program at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, told ABC News. "But I recommend every patient that I see should get vaccinated for influenza."
Standard-dose inactivated flu vaccines grown either in eggs or cell culture are available for anybody as young as 6 months old.
High-dose and adjuvanted flu vaccines, both of which are egg-based, are available for those aged 65 and older due to their higher risk of severe illness.
Anyone aged 9 and older can receive a recombinant flu vaccine, which is produced without eggs. For those between ages 2 and 49, who don't have certain medical conditions and aren't pregnant, a nasal spray flu vaccine is also available.
Additionally, in August, the Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine to protect those aged 50 and older.
One dose is recommended for children between 6 months and 8 years old who have received two doses in past seasons and everyone aged 9 and older.
Some children under age 9 may require two doses based on prior vaccine history.
Public health specialists told ABC News they recommend that people receive flu vaccines by the end of October, but that people should get the vaccine even if later in the fall or winter as long as influenza viruses are circulating and unexpired vaccine is available.
Dr. Majd Alsoubani, infectious disease physician at Tufts Medical Center, said that one thing she often hears from patients is that every time they receive the vaccine, they get the flu -- which she says is a combination of misinformation and misunderstanding.
"All the injectable influenza vaccines, they don't have the live virus, it only contains parts of the virus, so it doesn't cause influenza," she told ABC News. "We know that the vaccine needs a couple of weeks just to create protection, so if they were exposed to influenza before the vaccine or right after, they actually might get the flu because the vaccine didn't have time to provide that protection."
People aged 18 and older are recommended to receive the COVID-19 vaccine, as are children ages 6 months to 17 years old at increased risk
Parents of all other children should speak to their pediatrician to discuss getting the vaccine.
The updated 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccines target the XFG strain, a recombinant Omicron variant, meaning it formed through the combination of two Omicron subvariants.
Moderna's mRNA vaccine is approved for those 6 months through 64 years old with an underlying condition and for all adults aged 65 and older. Another Moderna mRNA vaccine that is a lower dosage is available for those ages 12 and older
Pfizer's mRNA vaccine is approved for those 5 years through 64 years old with an underlying condition and for all adults over age 65.
According to the CDC, underlying conditions placing people at risk for higher risk for severe COVID-19 include but are not limited to cancer, asthma, chronic lung disease, diabetes, heart conditions, mental health conditions and pregnancy.
Also available is a vaccine from Novavax, which is a protein-based vaccine, for those aged 12 and older.
Angarone said people can safely get the flu and COVID vaccine during the same visit if they are eligible.
"I recommend to my patients just get it at the same time, or if you don't want to get both at the same time, get [the COVID vaccine] a week apart from the flu vaccine," he said. "So, kind of around this time, October timeframe."
"The immunization recommendation kind of follows the people who are at risk of severe disease," Alsoubani said. "So the RSV vaccine currently is only one dose, so you're one and done. It's not an annual vaccine."
The CDC recommends RSV vaccines for all adults aged 75 and older and adults between ages 50 and 74 at increased risk for severe RSV.
It is also recommended for all pregnant people between 32 and 36 weeks' gestation.
For infants under 8 months who are in their first RSV season and whose mother did not receive a maternal RSV vaccine, two monoclonal antibody shots are available.
Monoclonal antibodies are proteins manufactured in a lab that mimic the antibodies the body naturally creates when fighting an infection.
A small group of young children between ages 8-19 months at increased risk for severe RSV may also be eligible.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.content_orig:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America,” and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/ Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of Republican governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title_orig: Republican midterm triage puts bleak outlook into focus
articles.title_zh: Republican midterm triage puts bleak outlook into focus
articles.content_orig:
The biggest donors in the 2026 midterm election are breaking decisively toward Republican candidates and causes, a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records found.
Fourteen of the 20 largest donors and donor groups this election cycle have exclusively or nearly exclusively backed GOP candidates or aligned groups, according to a CNBC analysis of federal campaign-finance records. Together, the 20 account for $1.2 billion, or about an eighth of the roughly $9.8 billion raised this election cycle through Sept. 25 across the campaigns and super PACs CNBC examined.
CNBC analyzed FEC records for contributions reported during the 2026 election cycle, covering Jan. 1, 2025, through the latest filings available, combining spouses and closely affiliated donor entities where appropriate and removing duplicate or superseded transactions. The analysis of disclosed federal political committee contributions provides the most up-to-date snapshot of who is financing the 2026 midterms and shows a stark divide in where the biggest donors are putting their money.
Democratic megadonors, meanwhile, are increasingly bypassing the national party, though in some cases they're giving directly to candidates instead.
With less than four weeks until Election Day , some of the biggest six-figure checks that once routinely flowed to the Democratic National Committee haven't materialized. Fundraisers told CNBC the hesitation reflects lingering 2024 election "trauma" from Kamala Harris' defeat, fears of democratic socialism and disillusionment with the DNC's leadership in Washington.
"We don't have the kind of donors they've got," said Matt Bennett of the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way. "The advantages that the Republicans have are enormous, and no amount of donor enthusiasm on our side is going to close that gap."
The Republican Party is scrambling to defend its congressional majorities as more House and Senate races once considered safe for the GOP have become competitive. From Labor Day through Sept. 25, conservative super PACs have outspent their Democratic counterparts $310 million to $174 million, a magnitude approaching 2 to 1, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC records.
"No one ever agrees with anyone on 100% of the issues, but we are doing really well fundraising," said Republican fundraiser Eric Levine, founder and managing member of ERL Federal Consultants. "My understanding is that a lot of this money is going to candidates that may have a little trouble raising their own money. One name that comes to mind is [Ken] Paxton in Texas."
Less than six weeks before Election Day, the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted 15 House races toward Democrats and said the GOP was on track to lose its House majority. The race for control of the Senate is closer but has also moved toward Democrats: Cook now rates control a " true Toss Up ," with Democrats needing four seats.
Democrats "are starting to see this real opportunity in a bunch of these races," said Caroline Welles , who leads The First Ask, a PAC supporting Democratic women, after working at the DNC from 2017 through 2022.
Republican money is coming from Wall Street financiers and industrial titans alongside a new wave of cryptocurrency , artificial intelligence and online gambling executives. The cash is flowing to candidates, super PACs and industry groups aiming to shape policy fights in Washington.
Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donors in CNBC’s overall top 20 groups are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC records. The previously unreported finding is a sharp increase from a comparable point in the 2022 midterms, when Republican-aligned donors accounted for 67 cents of every dollar from the top 10.
"Populist sentiment against billionaires is at a fever pitch, but they have more money and more impact than ever before," said Saurav Ghosh , the Campaign Legal Center's director of federal campaign finance reform. "It's the result of unchecked free-for-all spending, and evidence has shown it can swing close races." The group is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded by a former Republican FEC chairman.
Seven of the 20 largest donors and donor groups in CNBC's analysis have major ties to the crypto, AI or online gambling industries. Together, they have contributed roughly $377.1 million this cycle, CNBC calculated — nearly a third of the money from the 20 largest donors and donor groups in CNBC's analysis.
Venture capitalists Marc Andreessen , Ben Horowitz and their firm Andreessen Horowitz have put roughly $91.3 million into politics this cycle. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna , have given $50 million, while Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss have contributed roughly $55.1 million. Crypto.com operator Foris Dax Inc. has given $38.6 million. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , whose businesses include xAI, is another top 20 donor.
Those four donor groups alone have contributed roughly $93 million to President Donald Trump's flagship super PAC, MAGA Inc. , which entered September with $415.8 million in cash after spending little of the $424.4 million it reported raising since Jan. 1, 2025. Two Trump-aligned groups launched in September, No Going Back PAC and Safety & Affordability PAC, have booked about $140 million in House and Senate ad buys and reservations, according to AdImpact.
Musk has contributed roughly $90.6 million during this cycle, including more than $50 million to his America PAC , according to CNBC's calculations based on FEC filings. His super PAC has since reported nearly $27 million in independent expenditures across House and Senate races in the 2026 general election, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings.
Companies are also directing millions into political groups focused on fights affecting their own industries.
Coinbase and Ripple have contributed roughly $33.2 million and $48 million, respectively, to crypto super PAC Fairshake , which supports candidates from both parties whom the industry considers allies. That's more than half of Coinbase's political spending and 96% of Ripple's this election. DraftKings has similarly directed about $34 million of its nearly $35 million spent this election to Win for America , the sports-betting industry's super PAC, according to FEC filings.
"Crypto wants to position itself as a political kingmaker — spending heavily and making sure lawmakers know it," said Dustin Duong , a researcher at Americans for Financial Reform who has analyzed crypto and AI political spending this election cycle. "But much of that money has gone to candidates already well-positioned to win."
In Congress, crypto companies are pushing for market-structure rules , AI firms are battling over how Washington will regulate their rapidly expanding industry, and sports-betting operators are confronting regulatory fights .
As Republican donors open their wallets, some of Democrats' biggest benefactors are missing from the DNC's donor rolls.
George Soros — the only Democratic-aligned donor among the 10 largest individual and family donor groups in CNBC's analysis— and his son Alex have given the DNC nothing this election cycle. It's a reversal from 2022, when the two contributed more than $1 million to the committee, according to FEC filings. The two gave $1.125 million combined to the DNC and its joint fundraising committee in 2022, a total that would have ranked first among DNC donors in CNBC's analysis.
Elsewhere, Dustin Moskovitz , the Facebook and Asana co-founder gave roughly $413,000 to the DNC during the 2024 cycle, alongside $50 million to Future Forward and $929,600 to the Harris Victory Fund . CNBC found no contribution from Moskovitz to the DNC this cycle.
"Donors, just like voters, want to feel energized and enthused, and they're getting that from the candidates this cycle rather than the major groups and the party apparatus," said The First Ask's Welle

articles.title_orig: China pushes for equal dialogue in resolving trade differences with EU
articles.title_zh: China pushes for equal dialogue in resolving trade differences with EU
articles.content_orig:
Observers on both sides are braced for more turbulence – and mainly hope Beijing and Brussels can avoid a full-blown trade conflict
As China and the European Union began a fresh round of trade talks in Beijing on Thursday, observers on both sides appeared to agree on one thing: a big breakthrough was unlikely.
Chinese firms based in Europe said they hoped the talks could achieve some “limited progress” to help stabilise the trade relationship, while European analysts remained cautious about the potential outcome.
“They’re bound to get some results,” said a Chinese source with knowledge of the talks, adding that EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic “will not go home empty-handed”.
The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU called on both sides to make full use of the Trade and Investment Consultations (TIC) mechanism to manage differences, push for solutions and send clearer signals to businesses.

articles.title_orig: Long-Deployed Aircraft Carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln Set for Homecoming
articles.title_zh: Long-Deployed Aircraft Carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln Set for Homecoming
articles.content_orig:
The Defense secretary praised the ship's crew for its resilience and dedication.
The USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group will return to its homeport of San Diego on Thursday, concluding a 10-month deployment to the Middle East where it played a key role in the war with Iran and set a new record of 265 days in between ports of call.
In all, the ship will have spent 321 days on deployment, the second-longest since the end of the Cold War. The longest deployment was set earlier this year when the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford returned from a 326-day deployment to Europe, the Caribbean and the Middle East.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited the Lincoln on Wednesday ahead of its return home and praised the ship's crew for its resilience and dedication during the lengthy deployment.
Hegseth told sailors gathered on the carrier's flight deck that he had extended their deployment twice -- in recent years typical carrier strike deployments have lasted seven months.
"I plead guilty, A., because of the incredible effectiveness that you showcased on the battlefield and the necessity. But also B., the mission required it, and C., because President Trump had full faith that you would deliver on behalf of the American people, and you did" he, added.
"What the USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group did, no other carrier strike group has ever done," Hegseth said, listing its accomplishments: "10,000 sorties, 23,000 combat flight hours, almost 4,000 combat sorties, 1.5 million pounds of ordinance dropped on the enemy," to cheers from sailors.
The aircraft assigned to the carrier had returned to their home bases in California and Washington state earlier in the week.
The Lincoln's crew suffered from supply disruptions caused by the start of the war that impacted food stocks and the long deployment led to reports that the crew's mental health was suffering.
The Navy has reported that there were eight suicide attempts aboard the carrier during the deployment, including one sailor who jumped overboard and was later rescued.
That figure that appears to be on the lower end of what is experienced during carrier deployments, according to a U.S. official.
"There were a few folks in the media who tried to turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol," Hegesth said. "A symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale, or a symbol of a failed mission. And what I look out right here or when I talk to your leadership, and I haven't had a chance to talk to a number of you, I know it's the exact opposite."
At the conclusion of his remarks, Hegseth announced that the Lincoln carrier strike group was being awarded the prestigious Presidential Unit Citation, an award for distinction given to military units.
When he read the citation to the crew, he disclosed more statistics about the carrier group's air operations against Iran that have not previously been disclosed.
That included: 3,693 combat sorties, 1.37 million pounds of ordnance dropped on Iranian targets, the launching of 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles by warships accompanying the carrier, the shoot-down of 77 Iranian one-way attack drones and 21 anti-ship cruise missiles, the defense against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying dhows, and helping with the sinking of 64 Iranian warships.
Navy officials have said that the Lincoln's deployment has helped them make quality of life improvements for future lengthy carrier deployments, including that of the USS Theodore Roosevelt which left San Diego a week ago bound for the Middle East.
"Roosevelt is maximizing its load-out of food, retail products and hygiene items before getting underway," Adm. Daryl Caudle, the Chief of Naval Operations, said in a recently released video.
"The crew is converting available spaces into additional storage, building the ability to remain self-sufficient for longer periods, especially when resupply may be difficult," said Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman.
And quality of life is a focus with new entertainment equipment available to sailors. as well as more durable fitness equipmen. and spare cardio machines.
The carrier's systems are also being upgraded with software updates and instructions, and being pre-staged aboard the ship," allowing the crew to keep critical services running even when bandwidth is limited or the ship is operating in a degraded condition," Caudle said.
Improvements have also been made to climate control systems and a specialized team will be on board to inspect and optimize those systems, Perryman said.
And improvements are being made to keep families informed about the deployment.
"As one carrier returns home, we listen to its sailors and families. We capture what worked and what didn't, and we make it better the next time," Prettyman said. "To the Lincoln team, thank you for what you accomplished and for what you taught us, and to the Roosevelt team, we're doing everything we can to make sure you are ready for the mission. You and your families."

articles.title_orig: What impact Old Vine Seal can have on world’s oldest vineyards
articles.title_zh: What impact Old Vine Seal can have on world’s oldest vineyards
articles.content_orig:
What started way back in 2010 as a grassroots, volunteer effort by wine critic Jancis Robinson MW and her team to record all the vineyards in the world that qualify as old vines has developed into the full blown Old Vine Registry that now includes close to 5,000 producers. It has now introduced the OV Seal to give those producers the chance to promote, on their label, how old their vines are and help spread the word to wine drinkers about the importance and significance of old vines. Alder Yarrow, architect and manager of the OVR explains what he hopes the new seal can achieve.
Tell us about the new seal initiative you have introduced?
The creation and growth of the Old Vine Registry has always been predicated on the idea that we can’t preserve or value what we don’t know about. So our first and ongoing goal has been to catalogue old vine vineyards everywhere.
In addition to knowing they exist, however, to keep them in the ground we have to make sure they remain economically sustainable for those who farm them, and one of the ways to do this is to drive increased awareness and sales of the wines that get made from old vineyards.
In order to do that, the Old Vine Registry had to get out of the internet and into the real world, and the OVR Seal is our attempt to do that—to start having the conversation about old vines at the shelf level.
What do you hope to achieve with it that you can’t currently do with the Registry?
The Old Vine Registery now has the records of nearly 5,000 producers in its database
By allowing registered producers to put the OVR Seal on their bottles, we are giving wineries around the world the chance to declare how old their vineyards are and to give interested consumers a destination to learn more, in the form of the Old Vine Registry listing for their vineyard.
This offers an opportunity for consumers to learn and engage in a way that the use of words such as “vieilles vignes” or “old vines” don’t offer. Also unlike those terms, which mostly have no legal meaning or regulation guiding their usage around the world, the OVR Seal offers a more concrete and legitimate declaration that a vineyard truly is old.
What do producers or winemakers need to do in order to use the seal?
In order to use the seal, producers must have their vineyard(s) listed in the Old Vine Registry, which is free and easy to do. Once that has occurred, a producer must simply pay a one-time fee of $300 to get access to seal artwork that corresponds to the age of their registered vines.
They are then free to use the seal on their packaging and digital marketing materials associated with wines made from their registered vineyard.
You are launching the seal with a few initial producers - who are they and why have they come on first?
We teased the fact that the Seal was coming back in June, and a number of wineries immediately reached out asking how they might get access to the seal. We offered the opportunity to get early access to the seal to all the producers who made such inquiries, and eleven of them stepped up and said they wanted to particpate.
Derek Mossman Knapp of Chile's Garage Wine Company is one of the first producers to take on the Old Vine Registery seal
Our launch partners are: Seghesio Family Vineyards and Bedrock Wine Company in Sonoma, Garage Wine Company in Chile, Versado and Ciclo Andino in Mendoza, AYA Estate in Bulgaria, Sown Estate in Napa, Woldridge Creek Winery in Oregon, Methymnaeos Organic Vineyards in Greece, Plaimont in Gascony, and Tenuta Santa Maria in Soave.
These are all wineries that have, at a minimum, made commitments to making old vineyards a key part of their philosophical approach to winemaking. Some of them, like Bedrock Wine Company or Garage Wine Company, go much further than that, as shepherds of some of the world’s oldest and most storied vineyards.
How will producers be able to use it in their marketing and on their labels?
The seal is available for use in the context of products and marketing that are specific to one or more vineyards that are recorded in the Old Vine Registry. The age-specific seal can be used on wine packaging if 85% of the grapes come from one or more registered vineyards that are at least as old as the age-mark on the seal. In the same fashion, the seal may also be used on technical sheets or sell-sheets or even e-commerce product pages for specific individual wines.
We also anticipate producers using the seal in the context of marketing a specific registered vineyard, perhaps on websites or in print marketing, or even by putting a sign in the vineyard itself. We’re really open to however wineries want to use the seal, provided it is always in the context of mentioning or referencing a specific vineyard rather than generic marketing about the brand as a whole.
What percentage of producers who are in the registry do you hope to sign up to use the seal?
Examples of how producers are using the Old Vine Registry seal on their labels
We honestly have no idea how many wineries are going to be excited about this seal. Many producers don’t even know that their vineyards are listed in the Old Vine Registry. Of the 5,474 unique producers listed in the Old Vine Registry, if we got 10% of them using the seal, I would consider that a smashing success.
Is there a registration cost to use the seal?
Yes, we’ve settled on a one-time $300 registration cost to use the seal. This amount was chosen to be affordable to even the smallest producers, while making sure that everyone who registers has at least a little skin in the game. The fee is not a recurring subscription, and registered producers are free to use the seal providing they have a qualified, registered vineyard that is still in the ground.
For those that don’t know the Old Vine Registry - what are your primary objectives?
As a registered nonprofit, Old Vine Registry exists to catalog the world’s vineyards over 35 years-old. Once recorded, we hope to drive awareness of and an increased appreciation for the value of old vineyards with the hopes that this leads to increased sales of the wines they produce, and ultimately their preservation.
How do you hope the seal will help your overall work?
The seal will hopefully become a point of difference and an opportunity for conversation between producers and their customers that brings the idea of old vines and what makes them special into the spotlight. If using the seal can get some of wine lovers to be more curious about old vines and why they matter we’re on our way to the ultimate outcome, which would be to create a legitimate commercial category for old vine wines.
We’re working towards a day when every serious wine list, every retailer, importer, and distributor, should have an old-vine section that is used to highlight the incredible wines made from the world’s old vineyards.
What other initiatives do you have planned for the OVR?
Alder Yarrow is manager of the Old Vine Registry - a role he is prepared to do on a voluntary basis
Once the OVR Seal program is up and running smoothly, we’re going to go back to making improvements to the Old Vine Registry website that will make it an even more valuable resource for the industry and academia. This will include publishing analysis on the increasingly sizeable set of data that the registry collects and different ways of interrogating that data.
And of course, we’re going to continue adding more and more vineyards to the registry. We’re not anywhere close to having even a quarter of the world’s old vineyards catalogued.
In October of 2024, the OIV published Resolution OIV-VITI 703-2024 which for the first time established an official definition of what “old vines” means for European wine. More importantly that resolution recommended "the cataloguing of old vineyards and old grapevines" and "to make openly available official data from the vineyard register to draw up vineyard maps and ascertain the age of vineyards.”

articles.title_orig: Toss-ups, triage and targets: How to read the wide-open 2026 House map
articles.title_zh: Toss-ups, triage and targets: How to read the wide-open 2026 House map
articles.content_orig:
A general view of voting machines at the Franklin County Board of Elections on Oct. 6, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. Jeff Dean/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly .
With just under a month to go until Election Day, financial decisions made by both parties appear to suggest the question being asked is not if Democrats take control of the House, but how large the majority may be.
Currently, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 seat advantage. In February 2025, the Cook Political Report's initial ratings for the midterms found a small slice of 39 races listed as competitive, with 18 classified as "toss-ups."
That topline number has shifted, with Cook currently listing 43 districts as competitive, including 22 toss-ups. But beyond that, under the hood, Democratic and Republican groups are marshalling hundreds of millions of dollars to influence an electoral landscape that is much larger.
An NPR analysis of both parties' campaign targets, future ad reservations and outside spending by Trump-aligned super PACs finds more than 90 districts where resources are being committed in the closing weeks of the midterms.
Here's a look at the types of races that will decide who controls the House in 2027.
If the political environment remained unchanged from the 2024 presidential election, a small group of House races would be competitive no matter what, like the 10 districts that voted for one party's presidential candidate and the other party's House nominee. (Not counting those changed by redistricting in the last 18 months, but more on that below)
That includes the seats held by New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler (NY-17), Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01) and Washington state Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-03).Another group of seats had very close margins in 2024, like Democratic Rep. Adam Gray's victory by fewer than 200 votes in California's 13th Congressional District and a 799 vote victory for Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa's 1st Congressional District.
But this is not the same political environment as 2024. President Trump's unpopularity with voters has reached record highs, with the share of voters who strongly disapprove of his job performance sitting higher than any point in either term in office.
Voters are unhappy with the ongoing war in Iran, rising gas prices, tariffs and immigration enforcement, and a wave of anti-incumbent sentiment has driven a record number of Congressional retirement announcements along with a number of sitting lawmakers losing their primary races this year.
Other races to watch: CO-08, NY-03, PA-08, PA-10
Further scrambling the map: a redistricting arms race that resulted in new district lines for an estimated 1 in 10 registered voters across several states.
Republican-led state legislatures, at Trump's urging and in some cases threats, tried to draw new House maps that would give them multiple additional seats in states like Texas and Florida, while Democrats countered in California.
But many of the new district lines were drawn with assumptions made about voters who backed President Trump in 2024 and what they would do in 2026, and in some cases, could backfire.
According to Strength in Numbers/Verasight polling data shared with NPR, Trump has lower-than-average job approval in communities that make up newly-redrawn districts in South Florida and along the Texas-Mexico border, like TX-28 and FL-25.
In North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Rep. Don Davis saw his district that Trump narrowly carried in 2024 become even more conservative. But the national environment — and a U.S. Senate race where polls show Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper leading — has made the contest more competitive. More than $20 million in ad reservations are scheduled between now and Election Day in the rural and coastal district, making it one of the most expensive House races in the country.
Other races to watch: AL-02, OH-09, FL-22,TX-35
Heading into the final electoral sprint, there are sixty districts that are listed as priorities of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee along with Trump-aligned super PACs like No Going Back.
On average, those districts voted for Trump by an 8% margin in 2024, highlighting how deep into conservative areas competitive races have moved.
The DCCC has more than 90 districts on its battlefield map, including 46 targets to flip in its "Red To Blue" program, 26 "Frontline" incumbents in potentially tight races and another 19 it considers "Districts In Play."
The NRCC has 17 districts on its "Patriots" list of vulnerable incumbents to support and another 27 candidates in open races or challenging Democratic incumbents as part of the "MAGA Majority" program.
Not every race will ultimately end up close or see party control change hands. Many of the DCCC's "Districts In Play" gave Trump closer to 60% of the vote in 2024 and have seen little-to-no ad spend from either party.
Then, there are races like Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, where millions of dollars in spending has poured in from both parties — including from Trump-aligned super PACS — in a district Trump won by 15 points.
In Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, which Trump also won by 15 points, six-figure outside spending targeting Democratic nominee Chris Jones and boosting incumbent Rep. French Hill contributed to the DCCC adding that race to its "Red To Blue" target.
According to Ballotpedia tracking, the target lists compiled by the DCCC and NRCC are usually broader in their scope and limited in their success. From 2012-2024, the Democrats won a total of 34% of its target districts and Republicans won 29%.
In some races and places, Republicans and Democrats are beginning to pull back ad reservations for the rest of the year, according to data from ad tracking firm AdImpact, though for different reasons. The most high profile example for Republicans is halting the flow of money in the North Carolina Senate race and redirecting funds to Kansas.
Some House races have seen similar cancellations, too, like the open race in Nebraska's 2nd District that is both a DCCC Red To Blue and NRCC MAGA Majority target.
Still, that data shows close to half a billion dollars in ad reservations have been placed between now and Election Day, showing that in this midterm election neither party is taking anything for granted.
Other races to watch: FL-13, NC-11, OH-10, OH-15
