articles.title_orig: Bringing local models and sandboxed tools to Windows and GitHub Copilot
articles.title_zh: Bringing local models and sandboxed tools to Windows and GitHub Copilot
articles.content_orig:
Coming soon, GitHub Copilot will determine when a task is best handled by on-device intelligence and when it should leverage cloud-scale models.
When leveraging agents, developers need both choice and control. They need technologies that offer clear boundaries for their agents and make it easy to choose the model with the right speed, performance, and cost profile for each task. That’s why GitHub offers frontier models from major model providers, as well as options like Project HydraFusion , an orchestrator choosing one or multiple models for each task while balancing performance, cost, and latency. It’s also why Windows has developed Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) to help secure interactive and non-interactive agentic coding sessions.
Coming by the end of the month, GitHub Copilot will determine when a task is best handled by on-device intelligence and when it should leverage cloud-scale models. Rather than forcing developers to manage infrastructure decisions themselves, GitHub Copilot automatically coordinates local and cloud inference behind the scenes. For NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows PCs like Surface Laptop Ultra, that means we are enabling local coding in GitHub Copilot with powerful local inference models and hardware capable of delivering a great experience at the edge.
The result is poised to be the next step in the HydraFusion vision: intelligent orchestration that spans not just multiple models, but multiple compute environments including the edge. GitHub Copilot can run commands in these environments with controlled access to files, networks, system capabilities, and credentials. Developers can automate with confidence and security in mind.
Local inference starts with a memory budget. Surface Laptop Ultra is built around NVIDIA RTX Spark, with up to 128 GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of AI compute.
With a discrete GPU, dedicated video memory is an important constraint: moving model data between system memory and the GPU can add overhead. Unified memory gives the CPU and GPU access to a shared physical pool. That makes more capacity available to the workload, but it doesn’t make all of it available to model weights.
The operating system, your applications, and the inference runtime need memory, too. So does the key-value cache, which stores attention state for tokens the model has already processed. As an agent reads files and receives tool results, its context can grow, increasing memory use and the work needed to process the next request.
Keeping a model loaded between requests can avoid repeated loading work. However, it doesn’t guarantee constant response time; context length, memory pressure, and the rest of the workload still matter. That’s why the useful question isn’t just whether a model fits, but how it behaves over a complete coding task.
To bring this local-development experience to life, Microsoft AI developed a local version of MAI Code 1.1 Flash, a coding-optimized mixture-of-experts model with 137 billion total and 6.8 billion active parameters. The on-device work applies quantization and speculative decoding to reduce the model footprint and improve end-to-end responsiveness while preserving the task completion and tool-use quality that matter in an agent loop.
Quantization reduces the precision used to represent model weights and activations, lowering memory requirements. Because code doesn’t degrade gracefully, the release evaluation must measure coding-task success as well as footprint: a single incorrect token can produce a syntax error, wrong identifier, malformed tool call, or broken diff.
Speculative decoding trades additional working memory for higher decode throughput and lower end-to-end latency. A drafter proposes candidate token blocks and the target model verifies them.
For a coding agent, the important tradeoff is whether the smaller model can still complete the same tasks. A smaller footprint is useful only if changes in code quality and tool use are understood.
With our first shipping version of MAI Code 1.1 Flash on Surface Laptop Ultra we achieve the following performance at different context lengths, with peak memory usage of 75.5GB at 256k context. At 64k and 128k context, prompt-processing throughput reaches 923.5 and 769.8 tokens per second, respectively.
The quantized version of MAI Code 1.1 Flash we use on device retains capability impressively compared to the Bfloat16 cloud variant, coming in at 53GB, an 80% reduction in size.
GitHub Copilot is adding two ways to use local models across the GitHub Copilot CLI, Copilot app, and VS Code. Developers can let Copilot’s intelligent Auto orchestration choose when to use local or cloud inference, or they can explicitly select a local model for workflows that require direct control.
With Auto, developers do not need to decide where each task should be run. Across a multi-turn session, Copilot can consider task context and cache state as it routes work between local and cloud models, preserving useful, cached work as the session evolves.
This orchestrated experience complements direct model selection, giving developers a choice between letting Copilot optimize model placement and choosing a specific local model themselves.
Explicit local-model selection supports workflows that need a specific provider, model, or endpoint. Developers can select MAI Code 1.1 Flash through the Windows ML provider or connect GitHub Copilot to OpenAI-compatible local endpoints and choose from the models those endpoints expose.
An agent’s shell commands normally inherit the access of the account running them. Moving inference onto the device doesn’t change that. Sandboxing applies a policy to the processes and local services the agent launches, controlling access to files, networks, credentials, system capabilities, and execution paths regardless of which model requested the work.
GitHub Copilot uses Microsoft Execution Containers , or MXC, an open-source library from the Windows team that translates policy into native operating-system controls. On Windows, GitHub Copilot uses the BaseContainer tier of the ProcessContainer backend. On macOS, it uses Seatbelt. On Linux, it uses bubblewrap . These local backends don’t require a separate virtual machine or container image, but we plan to make them options available through MXC in the future.
When sandboxing is enabled, shell commands and, by default, local Model Context Protocol servers and language servers run inside the process boundary. Built-in file tools run inside GitHub Copilot itself: the agent harness checks their requests against the effective policy, but those checks aren’t OS-enforced child-process isolation. Remote MCP servers are also outside the local process sandbox; when MCP sandbox controls apply, GitHub Copilot checks their connection policy in process.
Opening the GitHub Copilot CLI and running `/sandbox` slash command allows you to configure your settings at any time.
To show how these technologies work together, let’s use a real-world example.
Consider a job that reads local repositories, runs their tests in working copies, and writes one HTML report each morning. The source repositories should remain read-only, and the test processes shouldn’t access the network. Model selection is independent: the same job can use a configured local or cloud model.
Open the settings dialog by clicking the gear icon in the GitHub Copilot app and selecting your project in the left menu. For this example, we’ll be using the `copilot-sdk` repo that hosts our opensource GitHub Copilot Runtime/SDK project.
Enabling the `Sandbox new sessions` toggle turns on sandboxing by default whenever you work within that project. By default, it’s current working directly is read/write while the rest of the system remains largely read-only or inaccessible to an agent.
Select the` Automations` section on the left navigation and click the `Start automation` button to open the dialog that allows you to configure a new automation.
Aft

articles.title_orig: World Health Organization says Russian lab worker’s death has not been clearly linked to plague
articles.title_zh: World Health Organization says Russian lab worker’s death has not been clearly linked to plague
articles.content_orig:
Frank McGeorge, MD , Local 4's Medical Expert
The World Health Organization says Russian authorities have reported no plague cases in the Irkutsk region.
The worker’s cause of death remains unclear.
A worker at a Siberian research institute that studies plague died after developing pneumonia, prompting officials to monitor and quarantine people who had contact with her and renewing questions about a disease many associate with the Middle Ages.
But Russian authorities have reported no plague cases in the region.
The World Health Organization said Russian officials described the worker’s illness as initially resembling a typical acute respiratory viral infection.
Officials have not publicly established the cause of death.
The worker died Oct. 2 at a hospital near Irkutsk, according to Reuters.
About 200 people who had contact with her were quarantined, and a local official said 60% had since been released.
Russian officials said no plague was found among the contacts who had been tested.
The WHO said it has been in contact with Russian authorities. Reports of the death have fueled speculation online, but Reuters reported there is no public evidence supporting the theories circulating on social media.
The incident has also revived memories of COVID-19.
But plague is not a new or unidentified disease. COVID-19 was caused by a newly identified virus; plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a well-studied bacterium that persists in animal populations in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas.
Dr. Leonard Johnson said plague persists in animal populations and continues to cause sporadic human cases around the world, including in the United States.
The CDC has said there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States from the Russian case.
There are three main forms of plague.
Bubonic plague, the most common, typically follows the bite of an infected flea and causes swollen lymph nodes.
Septicemic plague affects the blood; both it and bubonic plague are generally acquired through infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread through respiratory droplets from an infected person or animal, usually with close contact.
Pneumonic plague can be highly fatal if untreated, said Dr. Leonard Johnson, chief of infectious diseases at Henry Ford St. John Hospital.
But modern antibiotics can treat plague when given promptly. Johnson said people identified as close contacts of a confirmed case could be given preventive antibiotics, including doxycycline or ciprofloxacin, to reduce the chance of secondary infections.
He said the risk of wider spread remains low, particularly in the United States. That is a sharp contrast with the medieval epidemics that killed millions.
Experts remain cautious because they do not have direct access to the underlying information, and public statements by Russian authorities have not clearly established the cause of death.
So far, however, reports do not confirm plague or indicate a wider outbreak.

articles.title_orig: Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
articles.title_zh: Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
articles.content_orig:
The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump over television advertisements that were publicly funded and allegedly used to promote his political policies.
Ken Martin, who heads the Democratic Party’s leadership body, suggested in a statement on Wednesday that the ads were designed to bolster Republican odds in the upcoming November 3 midterm elections .
“Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November,” Martin said.
Later that day, Common Cause, a democracy watchdog group, filed a second lawsuit over the same set of ads.
It argued that the ads were “overtly political” and therefore ran afoul of laws that bar public funds from being used for political propaganda.
“These ads are not public-service announcements,” Common Cause said in its lawsuit, citing a justification Trump has offered for the television spots. “They are personal publicity and political propaganda through and through.”
Both lawsuits argue that, to create the ad campaign, Trump directed the White House to repurpose $20m in funds that Congress allocated for commemorative activities related to border security, including for those killed in the line of duty.
That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution.
“The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said.
The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriations bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”.
Both complaints seek to have the ads declared illegal, and the expenditures stopped. They also call for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads.
The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the Southern District of New York.
Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September.
So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.
Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his 2024 re-election campaign.
Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”.
The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.
On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular . Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them.
Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations.
But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that taxpayer funds would no longer be used for future ads .
He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads.
Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign.
Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

articles.title_orig: California woman accused of spying for China will be jailed while awaiting trial
articles.title_zh: California woman accused of spying for China will be jailed while awaiting trial
articles.content_orig:
LOS ANGELES — A California woman accused of acting as a Chinese spy inside the U.S. will remain jailed pending her trial after a judge sided Wednesday with federal prosecutors who argued that she poses a flight risk.
Wanying Zhang, 34, who sometimes goes by Heather, will remain in pretrial detention following the ruling by U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim. The FBI arrested her Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she could board a flight to China.
In a criminal complaint, prosecutors accused Zhang of spying on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his residence in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. Zhang, of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of downtown Los Angeles, hadn’t registered as a foreign agent as required, they said.
Zhang was represented in court Wednesday by veteran criminal defense attorney Craig Harbaugh, who argued she wouldn’t flee in part because of her strong family connections to Southern California, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said.
Zhang’s family had been willing to put up their home equity — valued at $700,000 — combined with bonds from her husband, his sister, his father and a family friend totaling $120,000 as an assurance that she would appear in court.
But prosecutors countered that she had “hundreds of thousands of dollars available to her” in China, as well as investments in a business and contacts that could allow her to flee easily.
“I don’t think it’s a very strong argument that she’s that tied to her family here,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Elbogen said, casting Zhang as a lying foreign agent with the skills and resources to evade detection and capture.
An investigation found Zhang attended China’s University of International Relations, which an FBI investigator said in court documents is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus.”
The charging document alleges Zhang had been communicating with a former classmate, who is now believed to be a Chinese official, through whom she had arranged an agreement to conduct surveillance of the Taiwanese president’s son. The document says she later captured photos, video and license plate information about him and sent them to her alleged Chinese handler.
She is alleged to have done all of that alongside an unidentified “Individual 1,” according to the complaint, who prosecutors said Wednesday had already fled to China two weeks ago.
Zhang wore a white jail jumpsuit and remained shackled for the entirety of Wednesday’s proceedings, a departure from her initial appearance Monday, when she was uncuffed and wore street clothes, with her hair neatly styled.
Wednesday’s hearing had several testy moments among prosecutors, Harbaugh and Kim, largely over whether Zhang’s pattern of one-way flights overseas was a credible defense that she wasn’t a flight risk and whether she had other U.S. properties to rely on for monetary assets.
Discussion in court revealed Zhang had disclosed only one residence to pretrial services, while her husband later revealed they owned two more, which her attorney said was a misunderstanding.
“She lied to pretrial services. She’s a real estate agent; she should know what properties she owns,” Elbogen countered.
Zhang is due back in court as early as Oct. 19 for a preliminary hearing — if federal prosecutors don’t indict her before then.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: CNBC Daily Open: Another Fed hike is on the horizon — but when?
articles.title_zh: CNBC Daily Open: Another Fed hike is on the horizon — but when?
articles.content_orig:
Hello, this is Justina Lee writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.
Meeting minutes released Wednesday showed that U.S. Fed officials expect interest rates to increase before year-end, but the meeting summary provided no indication of when specifically it would happen.
The U.S. Treasury selling $39 billion of 10-year notes in an auction knocked yields off their highs, while the S&P also pulled back from its record high on Wednesday.
South Korean tech giant Samsung posted a third-quarter preliminary operating profit that exceeded 100 trillion won for the first time in its history, while Lululemon poached Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger.
Traders are bracing themselves for another hike from the U.S. Federal Reserve this year, after meeting minutes released Wednesday showed that Fed officials expect to increase interest rates before the end of the year in order to fend off inflation that has run above target for more than five years.
However, the meeting summary did not show when the hike would occur – only that a stable labor market and persistently higher prices would likely lead to a second hike this year. Rates will be decided by the Fed on Oct. 28 and then again on Dec. 9.
Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury yields backed off their highs after the Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes in an auction. According to BMO, the sale was "strong," with higher than average bidding from non-dealers.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield reached its highest level since April 2002 at 5.365% on Wednesday. The 30-year bond yield also hit its highest level since May 2002 at 5.732%.
Meanwhile, the S&P also pulled back from its record high on Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.66%, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.22%. The Nasdaq Composite was 0.22% lower.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 0.92% lower. South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 2% and Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat. Mainland China market remained closed for the Golden Week holiday on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the spotlight is back on South Korea's tech sector, after Samsung Electronics posted a third-quarter preliminary operating profit of 107.40 trillion won ($80.2 billion). This is the first time in its history that the company has exceeded 100 trillion won, propelled by booming AI demand. Samsung is expected to release its full third-quarter earnings, including a breakdown by business division, later this month.
In the consumer sector, Lululemon said Wednesday that Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger is joining the company as president and chief product officer , with effect from later this month. The news comes as the athleisure space becomes increasingly competitive.

articles.title_orig: Trump returns to Texas, where Republicans are struggling
articles.title_zh: Trump returns to Texas, where Republicans are struggling
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in less than a month to stump for a Senate candidate who’s privately questioned his political capital and whom the president has publicly insulted in personal terms.
Such is the final sprint to the November 3 midterm elections as the GOP faces an increasingly uphill battle to hold on to the Senate, with the path to the majority running through Texas.
Republicans are pouring millions into bolstering state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who polls have shown is facing a closer-than-expected race against Democrat James Talarico in a state Trump carried by more than 13 points in 2024 and that hasn’t elected any Democrats statewide since 1994.
Trump’s Wednesday appearance in San Antonio, one Texas GOP strategist said, will be closely watched in the coming days for whether it can improve Paxton’s standing — which could determine continued investment in the state.
The president’s latest Texas trip — which comes less than a week after his last stop here — is part of an aggressive midterm travel blitz that has taken him to traditional red strongholds he overwhelmingly won two years ago, including Alabama, Oklahoma and Nebraska. The president has repeatedly told his rally crowds to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this fall, and his advisers believe their best hope for November is boosting base turnout .
But some Republicans , even in these red states, are looking for distance from the unpopular president. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott will not be at Trump’s Wednesday evening rally, citing scheduling conflicts. He skipped last week’s Trump appearance too.
“It’s pretty clear to me the Paxton team has made the calculation that they believe it’s absolutely worth it,” the Texas GOP strategist said.
But as Trump arrived Wednesday, Paxton is also making headlines for seeming to blame the president and some of his agenda for his struggles.
The GOP nominee told a group of donors and lobbyists last month that the Iran war and high gas prices are hurting his campaign, according to audio obtained by Axios on Wednesday. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said, according to Axios. CNN has not independently verified the audio.
Paxton’s campaign dismissed the story. “The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” spokeswoman Madison Cercy told CNN in a statement, adding that Trump “is doing everything he can to bring prices down.”
But that followed The New York Times last week publishing audio of Paxton complaining that Trump’s midterm convention, held last month in Dallas, wasn’t helpful.
“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” the Texas attorney general said. In a statement to CNN, Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux called the Times story “manipulated nonsense” to “create a story that doesn’t exist.”
Paxton has been plagued by his own set of scandals , including securities fraud charges, which ended in a pre-trial agreement; allegations of infidelity; and a 2023 impeachment in the state House (the Senate acquitted him). But that baggage didn’t stop Trump from backing Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.
Their relationship, however, has appeared fraught, even as Trump told reporters in the Oval Office earlier Wednesday that he has no regrets about backing Paxton.
At a stop in Denton, Texas, last week, the president called Paxton “one of the most loyal people” — but also “a pain in the ass sometimes.”
Then there’s his frequent ribbing of the state attorney general’s appearance.
“Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said during a speech at the Dallas convention: “I don’t.”
Trump did not repeat that refrain Wednesday night, calling Paxton a “fantastic man” as the two showcased warm relations on stage.
“I’m very proud of him and I think he’s gonna be an unbelievable senator,” Trump said as he invited Paxton to speak.
Paxton, in turn, expressed gratitude to his guest. “Aren’t you guys glad he came to San Antonio?” he asked an enthusiastic crowd.
The president “understands how important Texas is to efforts to try to keep the Senate in Republican control, so I think he can put all that aside and probably focus on the bigger picture,” said one Texas GOP operative unaffiliated with the Paxton campaign, granted anonymity to speak freely.
“But I’m sure he enjoys making Paxton squirm at the same time,” the operative added.
Asked about the candidate’s relationship with Trump earlier Wednesday, Paxton’s campaign pointed to his planned appearance on stage with the president.
Paxton’s comments reported by the Times underscore how the president’s unpopularity — his approval rating is 34% in the latest CNN Poll of Polls — may make him an unwelcome guest for some candidates.
And he is losing support among a group that helped propel him to victory in 2024. His approval rating among Latino voters was just 27%, according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll earlier this week. Trump may be looking to turn that tide with his visit to San Antonio, where the population is 64.6% Hispanic or Latino.
Trump sought to juice turnout among his MAGA base Wednesday evening with a focus on border security and other red meat issues. He attacked Talarico as a vegan — a claim the Democrat has denied. And there were visible efforts to organize, including information about early voting and mail-in ballots for attendees on screens and in handouts.
But Trump’s visit, the Texas Republican strategist said, comes with its own risk.
“Why go where you can potentially motivate the other side, rather than going to places like Lubbock or Amarillo or East Texas, where you can try to use that brand to actually motivate, you know, the type of voter that needs to turn out for Paxton to win?” the strategist said.
There were some signs of discontent. At least a dozen protesters, who interrupted Trump’s rally on several occasions, were removed from the event.
And Democrats see Trump’s return to Texas as a good sign for their side.
“If you have to pull in Donald Trump four times in the closing stretch of the campaign in Texas, then you have given up on independent voters. This is a loss mitigation strategy,” said one Texas Democratic operative.
The Senate race — and the GOP primary and runoff leading up to it — is already on track to be one of the nation’s most expensive.
The GOP-aligned bill in Texas is expected to exceed $300 million, with the party and its affiliated groups outspending Democrats by more than 5-to-1, CNN has previously reported . Since the end of the GOP runoff in late May, Republicans have spent $158 million on ads, with an additional $38 million in upcoming ad reservations, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Democrats, meanwhile, have spent about half that: $75 million on ads between late May and Tuesday, with $6 million reserved.
But that level of spending in deep-red Texas comes with consequences for the rest of the Senate map.
“A lot of us are very disappointed that our predictions have proven correct, and it’s going to cost somewhere between $100 and 200 million to save Ken Paxton as the Senate nominee,” said a Texas GOP strategist who had raised  concerns about Paxton during the state’s primary.
“If we save Ken and lose the Senate majority because we’ve lost Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Iowa and Ohio, the Monday morning quarterbacking is going to be biblical,” they added.
But Texas has seen close Senate races before, with Democrats’ hopes dashed at the ballot box. Eight years ago, Trump was a key surrogate for Ted Cruz when the senator faced then-rising Democratic star Beto O’Rourke. Cruz, unencumbered by the personal baggage Paxton is carrying this year, won his race by just 2.6 points.

articles.title_orig: Mamdani draws bipartisan backlash for criticizing Israel on Oct. 7 anniversary
articles.title_zh: Mamdani draws bipartisan backlash for criticizing Israel on Oct. 7 anniversary
articles.content_orig:
Israelis gathered in vigils across the country to remember the terror attack’s victims. In New York City, anti-Israel groups rallied and Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s post on the attacks drew criticism.
A group of anti-Israel protesters on Wednesday targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , calling him a "traitor," accusing him of "genocide" and claiming he "cannot weaponize being brown anymore."
The crowd of more than 100 demonstrators marched from City Hall to Union Square, where a vigil was held to mark the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks in Israel. The vigil was organized as an evening of mourning for those killed in the Oct. 7 attacks and the bloodshed that followed, including Israelis and Palestinians.
The anti-Israel crowd was just outside the barricades of the Israelis for Peace Vigil, beating on drums and attempting to drown out the speakers, according to City & State New York.
Mamdani was at the vigil and held a candle as protesters threw various insults at him, including accusations of genocide and "selling all your people out."
ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'
A group of anti-Israel protesters targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him a "traitor." (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)
"Zohran, what do you say? How many kids did you kill today?" the protesters shouted, according to the outlet.
"700,000 dead. Mamdani, your hands are red!" they also chanted.
"Traitor, traitor, come on out! You sold all your people out!" the group was also heard chanting.
The crowd also shouted: "Zohran, you can’t hide. We charge you with genocide!"
"We don’t care about where you’re from. You cannot talk about being Muslim anymore. You cannot weaponize being brown anymore. Identity politics can only get you so far," they said.
One protester also claimed to be a former intern for Mamdani, saying the mayor "was never working for the people."
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stands at a rally called by Israelis for Peace. (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)
Protesters also demanded that Mamdani take action against New York real-estate events that have marketed properties in Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which the demonstrators characterize as "stolen" Palestinian land, according to City & State New York.
"Mayor Mamdani, take a stand. Stop the sale of stolen land," the group chanted.
The protesters also called for abolishing the City University of New York's Board of Trustees, whose members are largely appointed by the mayor and governor. Protesters have previously accused the board of ignoring demands to divest investments linked to Israel and criticized its handling of anti-Israel demonstrations on campus.
Despite the protesters' accusations of genocide on Wednesday, Mamdani is a longtime critic of the Israeli government's actions in Gaza and has denounced its treatment of Palestinians in the aftermath of the 2023 attack.
MAMDANI SAYS IT WAS 'STRANGE' GETTING CALLED OUT BY NETANYAHU AFTER CALLING FOR HIS ARREST
An anti-Israel crowd was just outside the barricades of the Israelis for Peace Vigil, beating on drums and attempting to drown out the speakers. (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)
In a statement on Wednesday, Mamdani condemned Hamas’ attack as a "horrific war crime" while also characterizing Israel’s subsequent military operation as a genocide.
"The suffering did not begin nor end that day," he wrote. "It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children."
Israel has rejected accusations that it is committing genocide in Gaza, saying its military targets Hamas and other terrorist groups while seeking to minimize civilian casualties.
The mayor's statement sparked bipartisan backlash , with Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., calling it "egregious and insulting."

"There are 364 days of the year to focus on that. This is a day that should just be focused on what was by all agreement a horrific terror attack," Goldman, who is Jewish, told Politico. "What the mayor’s statement did today was to blame Israelis for the attack that they suffered three years ago. Regardless of what you actually think of the conflict and what’s happened either since or before, there’s no excuse for victim blaming."

articles.title_orig: A 194-year-old tortoise, world’s oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
articles.title_zh: A 194-year-old tortoise, world’s oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
articles.content_orig:
The world’s oldest-known terrestrial animal, an Aldabra giant tortoise named Jonathan estimated to be about 194 years old, may owe his extraordinary longevity to a combination of genetic traits and an ability to keep key cellular systems functioning in a more youthful way, according to scientists.
Members of this species are known to live more than 100 years, but Jonathan has far exceeded that. Brought to the remote South Atlantic island of St. Helena as a fully grown animal in 1882, likely from the Aldabra Atoll or the Granitic Seychelles, the tortoise now resides in a paddock at Plantation House, the governor’s residence.
“Other Aldabra tortoises have been claimed to have lived as long as Jonathan, but he has the most documentary evidence supporting his age,” said Benjamin Vaisvil, a researcher affiliated with the organization Kallel and co-lead author of the study published on Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.

articles.title_orig: Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says
articles.title_zh: Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says
articles.content_orig:
Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, GACA reported.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.
GACA said it is working “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities” to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
New cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport.
On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swathe of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones against Aden airport early on Wednesday. No casualties were reported.
Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

articles.title_orig: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government
articles.title_zh: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government
articles.content_orig:
President floats firing Chris LaCivita and James Blair over any ‘conflict’ after reports of work in Republika Srpska
Donald Trump distanced himself from two top advisers on Wednesday, claiming he did not have “any idea who else they work for”, after it was reported they spent the weekend assisting a pro-Russia government in the Balkans.
On Truth Social, Trump wrote that Chris LaCivita , the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, “are outside consultants” and “do not work for me other than as outside consultants”.
“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”
The president’s comments came after the New York Times reported that LaCivita and Blair traveled to Republika Srpska, an autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to assist the government ahead of elections over the weekend. Sources told the newspaper that each adviser was paid hundreds of thousands of dollars.
LaCivita and Blair are meanwhile working with Maga Inc , the Trump-backed SuperPac assisting Republican candidates in November’s US midterm elections .
Both men have long histories with Trump , and the US president has praised them separately on social media.
LaCivita joined Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign in 2022, after leading a pro-Trump Super Pac called Preserve America. In 2024, Trump wrote on Truth Social that LaCivita was “ THE BEST ” co-campaign manager alongside Susie Wiles, who now serves as the White House chief of staff.
Blair worked for Trump’s 2020 campaign in Florida and was the political director of Trump’s 2024 campaign. He joined the president at the White House as deputy chief of staff for legislative, political and public affairs.
In April, Trump called Blair “ one of the brightest political minds ” while announcing that Blair would leave his White House position, briefly, to join Maga Inc and assist Republicans in the midterms. Trump said Blair would return to the White House after the midterms.
Trump’s statement distancing himself from the two advisers comes as Maga Inc prepares to ramp up efforts to assist Republican candidates in next month’s elections.
after newsletter promotion
Public polls indicate Democrats are leading Republicans in several key competitive races . That is largely attributed to widespread disapproval over Trump’s handling of the economy and cost of living.
A spokesperson for Maga Inc told the New York Times that Blair and LaCivita remained engaged with midterm efforts while traveling, saying the two “hosted a team call with race captains on Saturday morning to go over recent survey data”.
The Guardian has contacted Maga Inc for comment.
Despite polling showing waning voter enthusiasm for Republicans, the party has a cash advantage over Democrats.
At the end of August, Maga Inc had more than $415m cash on hand. Several Super Pacs tied to Maga Inc have begun launching multimillion-dollar ad blitzes.

articles.title_orig: Levi Strauss Uses Tariff Refunds to Rekindle Consumer Business
articles.title_zh: Levi Strauss Uses Tariff Refunds to Rekindle Consumer Business
articles.content_orig:
Levi Strauss on Wednesday increased its profit outlook after it received tariff refunds, but gave less rosy revenue guidance.
The denim retailer raised its adjusted earnings per share expectation for the full fiscal year to between $1.54 and $1.56, from a previous range of $1.46 to $1.52. Analysts were expecting a range of between $1.52 and $1.59, according to LSEG.
The company also lowered its net revenue growth guidance for the full year to 7%, the bottom of its previously provided range of a 7% to 7.5% increase.
Shares of Levi were roughly flat in extended trading after initially rising.
For its fiscal third quarter, the denim retailer said it saw a 4% increase in net revenues in the Americas, though revenue in the U.S. decreased 1%. It also reported an operating margin of 13.8% for the quarter, compared to 10.8% in the same quarter last year, boosted by tariff refunds that contributed 4.9% to operating margin and gross margin.
Levi also said its tariff refunds contributed a 16-cent benefit to its earnings per share, of which 5 cents were "redeployed to support the business." On a call with analysts, CEO Michelle Gass said that money is going toward marketing and promotions during the holiday season.
Here's how Levi performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the three-month period ending Aug. 30, Levi reported net income of $168.6 million, or 43 cents per share, down from $218.1 million, or 55 cents per share, the year prior.
Sales rose roughly 4% to $1.61 billion from $1.54 billion last year.
Levi said direct-to-consumer net revenues increased 2% in the quarter, but comparable sales were roughly flat. DTC comprised 45% of total net revenue in the third quarter, the company said. On the other hand, wholesale revenues increased 6% for the quarter.
"While we delivered strong results across much of the business, our DTC performance fell short of our expectations during the quarter," Gass said on the call with analysts. "We have a clear understanding of what worked and what did not, and we have already taken targeted actions to improve performance."
The company previously said it's been seeing broad-based growth across its business segments, including its core Levi's and its premium blue tab.
Last month, the company announced John Vandemore will take over as chief financial officer effective Nov. 1, succeeding Harmit Singh, who announced his retirement in April.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street ends lower, off record highs, as Treasury yields climb
articles.title_zh: Wall Street ends lower, off record highs, as Treasury yields climb
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures were lower early Thursday, after the S&P 500 retreated from its record as yields spiked to multidecade highs.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures fell 132 basis points, or 0.26%. S&P 500 futures dipped 0.15%, and Nasdaq-100 futures were 0.21% lower.
Levi Strauss shares dipped almost 2% in extended trading after the denim retailer lowered its revenue growth guidance for the full year, though it also raised its profit outlook.
Wall Street is coming off a losing session. The S&P 500 dipped 0.2%, pulling back from an all-time high it reached just one day prior. The Dow fell more than 340 points, or 0.7%. The Nasdaq Composite slid 0.2%.
The Treasury on Wednesday sold $39 billion of 10-year notes, drawing solid demand with indirect bidders — including global central banks — taking more than 80% of the auction, above a 10-auction average of 72.4%. The sale helped the 10-year Treasury note yield ease off its 24-year high during Wednesday's session. The Treasury is set to sell $22 billion of 30-year bonds later Thursday.
The 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 4 basis points higher at 5.3178%, with the 30-year Treasury note yield up 4 basis points at 5.7064%.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 was down 1.12% while South Korea's Kospi lost 2.04%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.64% lower. Mainland China's CSI 300 declined 0.43%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index dropped 0.69%.
Higher yields have curbed investor appetite for equities in recent weeks, especially those parts of the market most hurt by higher borrowing costs. Industrials, for example, is the worst performing sector week to date.
Many investors are maintaining an optimistic view of the stock market, however. They expect that the start of earnings season could give the market the fuel it needs for the next leg higher.
In the third quarter, the S&P 500 is expected post a blended earnings growth rate of roughly 30%, which would be a third straight quarter of above-25% earnings growth, according to FactSet.
"If earnings remain strong, and the idea is that they probably will, if expectations are met and/or higher, that is going to sustain this rally — despite the fact that rates are higher," Courtney Garcia, senior wealth advisor at Payne Capital Management, told CNBC's " Closing Bell ." "It's not going to derail the market."
On Thursday, investors will await results from PepsiCo before the open. Traders will also watch for weekly jobless claims data.
HSBC's Hong Kong-listed shares fell 3.9% Thursday, following a report that the lender is planning job cuts in its U.K. wealth management business
The sweeping job cuts will include sharp reduction in specialist staff and financial advisors, as part of the bank's effort to expand AI integration, according to the Financial Times.
HSBC is in a "consultation period" over the proposed changes, the FT reported, adding that the affected employees are likely to exit the bank at the end of the month.
Oil rose Thursday as Middle East worries keep markets on edge, with the U.S. reportedly considering large-scale U.S. military operations in Iran in the coming weeks.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery gained 1.36% at $101.54 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November advanced 1.04% at $89.32 per barrel.
President Donald Trump and his national security team have talked about possibly restarting large-scale U.S. military operations in Iran in the coming weeks, NBC News reported, citing sources. That also includes the option of strikes prior to next month's midterm elections.
Meanwhile, tensions in the Middle East have been rising with Iran-backed Houthis recently targeting airports in Saudi Arabia, while Tehran has also been attacking tankers in the Hormuz Strait.
Asian stocks fell on Thursday. Japan's Nikkei 225 was down 0.4% while the broader Topix declined 0.8%.
South Korea's Kospi was down 0.35% and the small-cap Kosdaq lost 0.9%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.4%.
Asian stocks were poised to open lower Thursday, tracking losses on Wall Street as U.S. Treasury yields remain elevated and Federal Reserve minutes signaled another interest rate hike could be on the horizon.
Japan's Nikkei 225 was set to fall at open, with its Chicago and Osaka futures contracts last at 69,965 and 69,790 respectively, compared with the index's previous close of 70,035.71.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index stood at 23,962 lower than its last close of 24,130.5.
Minutes from the Fed's latest meeting, released Wednesday, showed most policymakers believed another interest rate increase would likely be appropriate before the end of the year, as inflation remained stubbornly above the central bank's 2% target.
The minutes, however, offered no indication of when the next hike might come, with officials emphasizing that future decisions would depend on incoming economic data.
Although the Federal Reserve's latest meeting minutes signal another interest rate hike by the end of the year, there's still a chance the central bank won't raise at all, Ameriprise's Anthony Saglimbene told CNBC.
"Higher interest rates may be doing some of the Fed's work, where they don't necessarily need to raise interest rates," the chief market strategist said. "That might allow them to kind of just staying pat for the rest of the year."
However, he added, "There's a lot of ifs in that statement, and I think it comes down to where interest rates settle out here over the next few weeks, because the market is already concerned that that's going to start slowing growth."
Levi Strauss shares dipped 2% in extended trading Wednesday night, after the denim retailer lowered its net revenue growth guidance for the full year — though it also increased its profit outlook.
The company lowered its net revenue growth guidance for the full year to 7%, the bottom of its previously provided range of a 7% to 7.5% increase.
It also raised its adjusted earnings per share expectation for the full fiscal year to between $1.54 and $1.56, from a previous range of $1.46 to $1.52. Analysts polled by LSEG were expecting a range of between $1.52 and $1.59.
— Sarah Min , Laya Neelakandan
Stock futures opened little changed Wednesday night.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures fell 8 points, or 0.02%. S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq 100 futures were both marginally higher.

articles.title_zh: A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop
articles.content_orig:

            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles

The laser-accessible nuclear transition in the thorium-229 isotope has been identified as a candidate for realizing an optical nuclear clock 1 that might outperform current optical clocks based on electron-shell transitions in atoms or ions 2 . It is expected to be more robust against external perturbations 3 , 4 and to provide enhanced sensitivity in clock-based tests of the fundamental principles of physics 5 , 6 . Here we realize a thorium-229 nuclear clock by stabilizing a continuous-wave laser to the 148-nm nuclear transition with rapid feedback based on absorption spectroscopy 7 . The thorium-229 nuclei are embedded in a millimetre-sized, room-temperature calcium fluoride crystal. A subharmonic of the 148-nm radiation is continuously compared with a Yb + single-ion clock. The nuclear clock shows a shot-noise-limited fractional frequency instability of \(3\times 1{0}^{-12}/\sqrt{\tau /{\rm{s}}}\) where τ is the averaging time, approaching 10 −15 instabilities over 1 day of operation. Improvements to the instability by several orders of magnitude are projected for future devices. We use the nuclear clock to constrain models of ultralight dark matter by searching for periodic fluctuations and slow drifts in the nuclear transition energy, on timescales between 20 s and 1 day. Benefitting from the enhanced sensitivity of the thorium-229 transition, these constraints compete with the best atomic clocks concerning dark matter coupling to photons and go beyond previous measurements regarding coupling to the strong force.
Over the last 70 years, atomic clocks based on microwave and optical electronic transitions have successfully served as frequency standards based on their high levels of stability and accuracy 2 , 8 , 9 , 10 . To elevate these atomic timekeeping devices to the next generation, in 2003, Peik and Tamm 1 proposed a nuclear clock based on the extraordinarily low-energy isomeric state of the thorium-229 ( 229 Th) isotope at 8.4 eV. With a lifetime approaching 1 h for a bare nucleus in vacuum, this transition offers a potential resonance quality factor of the order of 10 19 (ref. 11 ). Additionally, the nucleus couples only weakly to perturbative fields 12 , which allows the construction of an optical clock implemented in a solid material at room temperature 13 . By doping microgram amounts of 229 Th into a crystal host, an experimentally simple and robust clock can be created, offering a large gain in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared with approaches based on a single or a few isolated nuclei, while only moderately degrading the resonance quality factor 1 , 4 , 11 , 14 .
A clock based on the 229 Th nuclear transition is of great interest for testing theories beyond the Standard Model of particle physics that indicate that the fundamental constants vary over time 5 . The low energy of the 229 Th isomer transition originates from a coincidental near-cancellation of the mega-electronvolt-scale Coulomb and nuclear contributions to the binding energies of the 229 Th ground and excited states, making the transition frequency highly sensitive to fluctuations in the coupling constants of the interactions involved 5 , 6 , 15 . As a result, a solid-state nuclear clock in its development phase would already be competitive with or may even surpass the sensitivity of advanced comparable atomic clocks in the search for dark matter.
The realization of a nuclear clock builds upon half a century of scientific discoveries. See the reviews in refs. 12 , 16 . In a research stream initiated by Kroger and Reich in 1976 (ref. 17 ), the energy of the 229 Th nuclear transition was narrowed down from an originally conjectured value of below 100 eV to −1(4) eV (ref. 18 ), 3.5(1.0) eV (ref. 19 ) and then 7.8(5) eV (refs. 20 , 21 ) using gamma spectroscopy. Using the internal conversion decay channel, the existence of the 229 Th isomer was proven in 2016 (ref. 22 ) and the energy value refined to 8.28(17) eV (ref. 23 ). An optical detection of the 229 Th radiative nuclear decay was realized in 2022, which determined the isomer energy to be 8.338(24) eV (ref. 24 ) in the vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) range. Thereafter, resonant laser excitation in Th:CaF 2 , Th:LiSrAlF 6 crystals and ThF 4 and ThO 2 thin films was reported in 2024 and 2025 (refs. 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ), quickly followed by the resolution of the nuclear quadrupole structure in Th:CaF 2 (refs. 13 , 29 ).
The development of 148-nm continuous-wave laser systems in 2025 (refs. 30 , 31 ), in combination with highly doped 229 Th:CaF 2 crystals 32 , 33 , has enabled the measurement of the nuclear transition with absorption spectroscopy 7 . With this technique, it became possible to probe the 229 Th nuclear transition continuously, without being limited by the long isomeric state lifetime of approximately 10 min. Moreover, absorption provides a higher detection efficiency, yielding three orders of magnitude more signal photons per second compared with fluorescence.
An optical clock is based on an atomic transition with a narrow linewidth, which is probed by a clock laser with a long coherence time. By stabilizing this laser to the atomic resonance, it can inherit the desired stability and reproducibility from the atom. Aiming for millihertz resolution and accuracy, the feedback times in this process typically extend to several seconds, requiring a pre-stabilization of the laser for higher-frequency noise to an optical cavity that has a suitable short-term stability. With the combination of these two control loops, very stable laser frequencies can be generated and then converted into a time signal through a frequency comb acting as an optical clockwork 34 .
Here, we transfer this concept from an atomic to a nuclear reference transition. Although previous studies 7 , 13 , 14 demonstrated that it is possible to excite the 229 Th nucleus using VUV lasers stabilized to external frequency standards, it has not yet been possible to construct a system in which the laser interrogating the 229 Th nuclei is steered by the nuclear transition itself. Our system is a nuclear clock that operates as a stand-alone device.
The nuclear clock is composed of a cavity-stabilized laser for short-term stability (referred to as the clock laser) and a 229 Th interrogation system providing long-term stability (Fig. 1a ). We use a continuous-wave VUV laser source to interrogate the 229 Th nuclei 7 , 30 . This laser source comprises a 1,187-nm frequency-quadrupled commercial laser (the seed laser in Fig. 1 ) and a single-pass second-harmonic-generation stage using a randomly quasi-phase-matched strontium tetraborate (SBO) crystal. The frequency and linewidth of the 1,187-nm interrogation laser are determined by an offset phase lock to the clock laser. We modulate the offset lock frequency to perform absorption measurements. For the clock laser, we use a high-finesse cavity-stabilized external-cavity diode laser operating at 1,187 nm. The stabilization of the clock laser to the cavity uses a Pound–Drever–Hall scheme on a sideband generated by an electro-optical modulator, allowing us to shift the frequency of the clock laser independently of the cavity resonances.

articles.title_orig: Webull Stock Falls 20% Over China Ties: Who Really Controls the App?
articles.title_zh: Webull Stock Falls 20% Over China Ties: Who Really Controls the App?
articles.content_orig:
Digital investment platform Webull , which counts 28 million global users , is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to U.S. finance, according to a bipartisan congressional panel's findings shared exclusively with CNBC.
The bipartisan House Select Committee on China in its new report being released Wednesday found "a profound gap" between Webull's public marketing as "an American company" and actual control of the St. Petersburg, Florida-based firm.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the committee found.
The panel asserted that national security concerns around the company have "escalated" since October 2025, when Webull began carrying customer cash directly, according to a regulatory filing the panel cited. The committee alleges that creates a "structural exposure of billions of dollars in American capital."
The committee said the company's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. And those laws in China can compel firms to cooperate with the government in myriad ways, including data transfers.
Webull took issue with the report, saying via a spokesperson, "It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull." "Webull's U.S. business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida and its office in New York City, while U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S.," the spokesperson said via email. "We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide."
Webull's stock plummeted 18% in morning trading.
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., told CNBC in a statement that Webull's "China-based operations put American investors and their data at risk."
"Using technology providers in mainland China and an opaque China-linked ownership structure, Webull exposes its data to our foremost adversary," said Moolenaar, who chairs the House committee that issued the report. "Investors should heed this information when choosing who they do business with."
Webull, which trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange, says it operates a "global network of licensed brokerages," offering investment services in 18 markets around the globe. The online brokerage says it provides retail and institutional investors with 24/7 access to global financial markets. Users of the platform can trade global stocks, exchange-traded funds, options, futures, fractional shares and digital assets on the service.
Former Alibaba and Xiaomi manager Wang Anquan founded Webull in 2016 . Its competitors include Robinhood , Charles Schwab and E-Trade .
The congressional committee, which had requested information from the company in 2024, said Webull represents a national security risk because "critical backend systems, personnel and data flows may remain exposed to the Chinese Communist Party's mandatory intelligence laws and coercive demands."
The committee said in its report that Webull Financial's "intricate corporate and technology framework" is tethered directly to China.
Webull Corp. is a Cayman Islands-incorporated holding company, and the report found it holds $24.6 billion in customer assets. And although the company has a U.S. holding company known as Webull Holdings (US) Inc., the report says the company's technology structure also includes Webull Technologies Pte. Ltd, which is a Singapore-based entity. And the report says Webull uses a mainland China-based subsidiary that supports technology development and platform operations. The company traces its origins to Hunan Fumi Information Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese company that originally launched the business.
The release of the report comes on the heels of a largely friendly summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in September, and it comes ahead of further meetings between the two leaders later this year. It reflects concerns on Capitol Hill that the Chinese government could be planting seeds inside the U.S. financial system that could later be used to disrupt the American economy in the event of further conflict.
The committee also alleges Webull misrepresented the number of its China-based employees. In the report, the committee said the company initially told the committee it "does not have any offices or employees based in the PRC," and that "all Firm employees are located in the United States." But the committee says the firm remains operationally concentrated in China, with its mainland subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, growing to 863 employees, or 62% of the company's global workforce.

articles.title_orig: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.title_zh: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported.
The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS.
US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny.
The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan ​which brought the charges.
Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports.
Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges.
Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York.
The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.
The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term.
Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States".
Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.

Guilfoyle, 57, now the U.S. ambassador to Greece, begged for a cash infusion from Eric Deters, a 63-year-old former congressional candidate from Kentucky, he tells the Wall Street Journal , which also reviewed alleged Signal texts between the two.
Deters released a dossier of photos with Guilfoyle during the time in which he was paying her.
âIt wonât show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,â the Trump-appointed Guilfoyle texted Deters, according to the Journal. âPlease.â
In another message shared with the Journal, she allegedly wrote: âHoney please I need you to get this done for me today. You could just send it here.â
This is the message Guilfoyle sent to Deters asking for the money saying "It won't show up anywhere of you wire money to American Express..."
The Journal reports that the latter text, complete with a prayer hands emoji and a PDF with bill payment instructions from American Express, was sent on July 3, 2025, less than a week before her July 9 confirmation hearing.
The texts came as Deters was seeking Guilfoyleâs help in âgetting the attention of the new Trump administration on some personal tax and legal issues,â according to WSJ.
Among the pictures of Deters and Guilfoyle are images from the Kentucky Derby.
Deters ultimately did not make the payment. He says he told Guilfoyle, then still freshly split with Donald Trump Jr., that doing so would end his marriage. However, the Journal reports that in one message, Deters wrote that he has paid Guilfoyle $300,000 over the years and had ânot received one favor.â

Guilfoyle responded that Deters needed to stop creating a paper trail.
Deters and Guilfoyle posed for photographs together repeatedly.

The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Daily Beast.
Deters appeared in a series of photographs with Guilfoyle when they met.
Guilfoyleâs lawyer, Jesse Binnall, told WSJ that he disputes the messagesâ authenticity, but declined to provide specifics to the paper. He said Guilfoyle âwas owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events.â Deters denies he owed Guilfoyle anything.
A U.S. Embassy official told the Journal: âGuilfoyleâs career in and out of public service is guided by deep and abiding values. The bipartisan Senate Foreign Relations Committee fully vetted her, and the U.S. Senate confirmed her. The Ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity.â
However, in texts reviewed by WSJ, she appeared aware of the seriousness of her dealings with Deters.
âItâs unbelievable when we have a private arrangement with you that you would now CC a producer talking about money,â she allegedly texted him, upset that Deters told a producer on her podcast about their deal. âDo not say we have any arrangement.â

articles.title_orig: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.title_zh: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.

The project ensures that UW–Madison’s efforts at IceCube remain at the forefront of neutrino astronomy for years to come.

articles.title_orig: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.title_zh: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.content_orig:
After 58 years, Fuller Bazer, Ph.D., a University Distinguished Professor in the Texas A&M College of Agriculture and Life Sciences Department of Animal Science , will close out his scientific career in October.
During his groundbreaking tenure, Bazer also held joint appointments in the College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences Departments of Veterinary Integrative Biosciences and Veterinary Physiology and Pharmacology ,
“Dr. Bazer has built an enduring legacy as one of the foremost reproductive scientists in the world,” said Clay Mathis, Ph.D., head of the Department of Animal Science, “Dr. Bazer may be retiring, but his innovative work that transformed our understanding of pregnancy establishment in livestock will continue to have an impact on the industry for many years to come.”
Bazer is a Regents Fellow, Distinguished Professor, Presidential Impact Fellow, and the O.D. Butler Chair in Physiology of Reproduction, as well as a top researcher in the world in the “Animal Science and Veterinary” category, as named by Research.com .
At 88, he is ranked, according to Google Scholar, as the most highly cited researcher in the field of reproductive biology. He is credited with discovering uteroferrin, a phosphatase, produced in response to progesterone that transfers iron to the developing embryo and stimulates red blood cell development. He also identified estradiol as the pregnancy recognition signal in swine and interferon tau as the signal in ruminants — findings that have reshaped animal management practices to improve pregnancy outcomes.
Those findings were published across 58 years, from 1968 to 2025, averaging 16.9 papers a year, with 46 of the 982 publications appearing in the last two years.
Bazer earned his bachelor’s in biology from Centenary College of Louisiana, his master’s in animal science from Louisiana State University and his doctorate in animal science from North Carolina State University. He was a member of the Department of Animal Science, University of Florida from October 1968 to 1992 before joining the Texas A&M Department of Animal Science on May 1, 1992.
In addition to maintaining highly productive research and teaching programs, Bazer served as director of the Center for Animal Biotechnology and Genomics, 1992–2001; director of the Institute of Biosciences and Technology, Texas A&M University and Texas A&M Health Sciences Center, Texas Medical Center, Houston, 1994-2001; the inaugural vice president for research and interim dean of the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, January 1999 to December 2000, Texas A&M University System Health Science Center.
He also served as the associate vice chancellor and associate director of the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station, and executive associate dean of the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, January  2001 to December  2004; associate vice president for research, January 2005–December 2008; interim department head, Department of Veterinary Pathobiology, May-February 2010; and the World Class University Professor, Biomodulation Major, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea, March 1, 2010 to Aug. 31, 2013.
Bazer has had an outstanding career and significant impact on livestock fertility and reproduction, signified by his recognition as the recipient of the 2003 Wolf Prize in Agriculture for his interferon tau discovery as well as his discovery of other pregnancy-associated proteins. Additionally, he received the Alexander von Humboldt Award in Research in 2000. These are two of the highest awards in the field of agricultural sciences.
Bazer is also past recipient of the highest awards from each of his scientific societies: the Carl Hartman Award from the Society for the Study of Reproduction in 2004, the Morrison Award from the American Society of Animal Science in 2014, and the Marshall Medal from the Society for Reproduction and Fertility in 2025. He is also a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and a recipient of the L.E. Casida Award for Graduate Education and the Animal Physiology and Endocrinology Award, both from the American Society of Animal Science. He earned awards for research, graduate education and service from the Society for the Study of Reproduction.
