articles.title_orig: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules
articles.title_zh: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules
articles.content_orig:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.
The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.
For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.
But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.
In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.
You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.
And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.
When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.
So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.
The development of the Thalidomide drug is an example of this. In the 1950s it was prescribed to pregnant women suffering with morning sickness. But it is a chiral molecule - the right-handed version is an effective treatment, but the left-hand is toxic.
The original drug given was a mixture of the two, and it was later discovered that the body will convert between the two. The result was thousands of children, born to women who took the drug, developed severe disabilities.
Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."
By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule.
Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously.
"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible.
Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule.
In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed.
"Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat".
At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field.
Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society".
"Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added.
Prof Angus Davison, from the University of Nottingham, studies the biology of chirality and said that the Nobel-winning chemistry could help reveal how and why life favours "one-handedness".
"In ways that we don't yet quite understand, the chirality of the basic building blocks of life ends up making bodies that are themselves also chiral," he told BBC News.
This was the foundation, he explained, of our hearts being on left hand side of our bodies and snail shells that coil to the right.
Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said the research awarded this year's prize has become part of "our basic understanding of how chemistry functions".
He said showing how a mirror image is created is "probably the most fundamental question in life - because somehow that happened four billion years ago when life was created. And now we have, for the first time, mimicked that in the lab".

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | France Considers Issuing More Shorter-Term Debt After Bond-Market Turmoil
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | France Considers Issuing More Shorter-Term Debt After Bond-Market Turmoil
articles.content_orig:
France’s unprecedented wave of student protests has laid bare the country’s growing financial pressures, which will only become more difficult to tackle as Europe’s second-largest economy tries to rein in a ballooning budget deficit.
The country’s finances are in a precarious state. Public debt was more than $4 trillion in June, exceeding the size of the economy, according to the country’s statistics agency . The cost of servicing that debt has climbed by billions of dollars on last year, as bond yields spike .
At the same time, demands on the public purse are rising: Pension costs have climbed because of an aging population while the government looks to spend more on defense.
High school students, meanwhile, have called for a fix to staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure.
Solutions to France’s financial troubles have led to social unrest in the past. Efforts to raise the retirement age sparked widespread protests in 2023 .
French school protests grow as workers join students
Last week, the French government proposed deep spending cuts and tax hikes aimed at narrowing the budget deficit, but bond buyers are concerned that fiscal measures may be watered down by lawmakers ahead of presidential elections next year, said Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at consultancy Capital Economics.
The election could see President Emmanuel Macron ousted by either a far-right or far-left successor, raising questions over the country’s commitment to fiscal discipline. While Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally recently proposed substantial spending cuts meant to stabilize the public finances, her party also remains committed to costly tax reductions, Kenningham said.
“Investors will also be concerned about greater fiscal populism after the elections,” he wrote in a note last week. “There is a big risk that spreads rise a lot further, either before or after next year’s elections.”
Worries about a potential debt crisis in France boiled over last week, leading to a selloff in French bonds and a sharp rise in yields.
The spread between French and German bond yields expanded to its widest level since 2012. That difference in yields means investors are demanding much higher returns to hold debt from France compared with Germany, which is deemed a safer alternative.
The French bond rout has sparked fears of spillovers to other high-yield European debt markets, with some analysts drawing parallels with the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s .
Global bond sell-off deepens, sending borrowing costs higher around the world
Given France’s size and systemic importance, “the potential for contagion into other countries and the Eurozone at large is very large and could potentially cause a serious crisis for the entire region,” Angel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, an advisory firm, told CNN.
These worries in large part pushed the euro to its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025 on Monday. The currency, shared by 21 countries in the European Union, is worth around $1.12, having briefly dipped below that level.
The latest ructions in markets could weigh on a fragile economic recovery in Europe, bolstered by investment into artificial intelligence, stronger demand for European exports and higher defense spending in Germany.
Recent survey data showed that activity in manufacturing and services in the euro area increased at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years last month.
“(Economic) growth is staging a comeback and Europe has shown surprising resilience,” economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a late September note.
Fall of yet another premier will make it hard for France to fix its finances. What’s behind its debt problem?
High bond yields are a clear risk to that growth, however.
If governments don’t cut spending , “interest rates will continue to go up,” Carsten Brzeski, head of macroeconomics at Dutch bank ING told CNN.
Higher bond yields push up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy, making home and car purchases more expensive and driving down investment. They also make it more expensive for governments to borrow money and force a certain degree of austerity to stop yields from rising further.
Yields on French, German and UK government bonds have broken multi-year records in recent weeks as concerns mount about the sustainability of public debt loads.
Europe’s public finances pose “serious risks to eurozone financial markets and to the economy,” Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics, told CNN.

articles.title_orig: Indie Selects for October 2026: Discover and Progress Through Unforgettable Worlds
articles.title_zh: Indie Selects for October 2026: Discover and Progress Through Unforgettable Worlds
articles.content_orig:
Every Wednesday, dive into the Indie Select Hub — your gateway to a fresh, curated indie collection plus four themed spotlights that rotate weekly! You can always find this collection hub in the XBOX Store and on XBOX.com/IndieSelects.
Halloween has never been just about scares. Sure, there’s plenty of room for heart-pounding frights, but it’s also a season that celebrates imagination, creativity, and stepping into worlds beyond the ordinary. This month, indie developers embraced that spirit in unforgettable ways.
For October, the ID@XBOX team has curated six standout Indie Selects that invite you to discover mysterious realms, conquer new challenges, and uncover stories waiting to be told. From epic battles and eldritch horrors to cozy puzzles and island adventures, each game offers a richly crafted world filled with surprises around every corner.
So, whether you’re seeking thrills, mystery, or a new adventure to get lost in, here are this month’s Indie Selects (in no particular order):
Mortal Shell II is still unapologetically challenging, but combat feels faster and more aggressive this time around. The removal of the traditional stamina gauge means encounters aren’t simply about waiting for a bar to refill. You can stay in the fight, combining melee weapons, sidearms, abilities and brutal executions. It makes combat feel considerably more fluid than before.
The world has grown too. Rather than simply pushing you down a predetermined path, Mortal Shell II encourages exploration across a compact, interconnected open world filled with hidden areas, dungeons, weapons, upgrades and, naturally, plenty of horrible things waiting to ruin your afternoon.
What I particularly enjoy is that exploration feels connected to progression. Finding another Shell isn’t just another collectible checked off a list. It can completely change how you approach the game. Weapons offer extensive upgrade paths as well, giving you plenty of room to shape your own approach to combat.
Mortal Shell II certainly isn’t interested in making life easy for you, but there’s something satisfying about gradually turning the tables. You go from cautiously approaching every new enemy to becoming the nightmare wandering through their world.
If you enjoy dark fantasy, exploration, challenging combat and the satisfaction of mastering a game that initially seems determined to destroy you, Mortal Shell II is absolutely worth having on your radar.
If you’ve ever wondered what it would be like to assemble your dream team of benders and settle legendary rivalries yourself , Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game is ready to make that happen. This 2D tag-team fighter brings together iconic characters from “Avatar: The Last Airbender” and “The Legend of Korra,” combining elemental bending, flashy special moves, and fast-paced team combat into an experience that’s easy to jump into and rewarding to master.
As a longtime fan of the Avatar universe, this game immediately grabbed my attention. There’s something incredibly satisfying about watching beloved characters leap from the screen into a fighting game that feels so true to the world they come from. From the first match, I found myself grinning at familiar abilities, character interactions, and bending styles brought to life in exciting new ways.
What impressed me most is how distinct every fighter feels. Experimenting with different team combinations kept me coming back for “just one more match” as I discovered new strategies and synergies. Fans of games like Dragon Ball FighterZ , Marvel vs. Capcom , and Power Rangers: Battle for the Grid will recognize the thrill of building a team and learning how each character complements the others.
There’s plenty to learn with its tag mechanics and assists, but the journey of improving feels rewarding and keeps every victory exciting. Whether you grew up with “Avatar: The Last Airbender,” fell in love with “The Legend of Korra,” or simply enjoy energetic team-based fighting games, Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game captures the heart of the franchise while delivering a fun and action-packed experience that’s hard to put down.
From the moment I started playing Mewgenics , I knew I was in for a wild ride. From Edmund McMillen, the developer behind The Binding of Isaac , Super Meat Boy , and The End is Nigh , Mewgenics is a roguelike tactical turn-based RPG presented in a unique and cartoonish macabre art style, filled with dark humor and clever references.
Mewgenics offers a staggering amount of content that easily demands over a hundred hours of playtime, complete with deep strategy and a generational breeding system (yes, you breed mutant cats).
The game hooks you right away with its chaotic setup, you’re managing a house full of mutated cats and sending them out on tactical, grid-based runs. Every item, skill, and attribute is randomized, meaning no two runs ever play out the same way. When your cats survive a brutal dungeon crawl, they bring back scars and mutations that you can pass down to future generations. Breeding the ultimate mutant cat squad and trying to balance their weird genetic traits became an obsession.
The dark and sometimes graphic humor and the relentless difficulty might not be for everyone, but for me, it hit the right buttons. Mewgenics easily eats dozens of hours, keeping you hooked on trying just one more run. Mewgenics creates something entirely fresh, endlessly repayable, and wonderfully grotesque, fur-real!.
The Sinking City 2 takes the series in a bold new direction, delivering a third-person Lovecraftian survival horror experience set in a flooded 1929 Arkham. The story follows Calvin Rafferty as he searches for a way to save his fiancée, Faye, who has been trapped in a supernatural slumber after a ritual gone wrong.
From the moment I stepped into Arkham’s flooded streets armed with little more than a flashlight and a pistol, the game nailed its horror atmosphere. Traveling between districts by boat gives the city an open feel, while interconnected environments, puzzle-solving, investigation mechanics, and scarce resources keep the tension high.
What truly sets The Sinking City 2 apart, however, is its enemy design. Familiar Lovecraftian creatures provide plenty of frantic encounters, but the real stars are the Slither: parasitic worms that survive after their host dies. If ignored, they can crawl into nearby corpses, reanimate them, and force you to fight the same enemies all over again. This simple but brilliant mechanic transformed every multi-enemy encounter into a desperate scramble and created a constant sense of dread.
I don’t think I sat down once while playing The Sinking City 2 . Between its unsettling atmosphere, intriguing mystery, satisfying survival horror gameplay, and genuinely frightening enemies, it stands out as one of the genre’s most memorable experiences and a must-play for horror fans.
Woodo is that takes the cozy puzzle genre and turns it into something closer to a child’s toy box coming to life as it tells you a story. The puzzles put you in the position of assembling handcrafted wooden dioramas piece by piece, watching each empty, colorless scene slowly fill with detail, animation, and life as you click objects into their correct spots. It’s a small, tactile premise, but it’s executed with a level of care that makes every placement feel extraordinarily satisfying.
The narrative at the heart of Woodo is a story about Foxy, a city girl sent to the countryside for the summer, and her growing friendship with a local villager, who happens to be a frog named, well, Ben the Frog. The narrative unfolds across a series of interconnected dioramas, each one capturing a different moment from their shared adventure, guided by a warm, friendly narrator’s voice that makes the whole experience feel less like a puzzle game and more like a warm, cuddly bedtime story. articles.title_orig: World Commemorates October 7 Ahead of Christian Summit
articles.title_zh: World Commemorates October 7 Ahead of Christian Summit
articles.content_orig:
Stand for Israel | October 7, 2026
Three years ago today, Israel and her people endured the most horrific acts of terror in the nation’s modern history on October 7, 2023. The Holy Land held its National Day of Remembrance earlier this week, but Jews and Christians in the U.S. and around the world are taking today to remember the more than 1,200 victims, the 251 people who were kidnapped, and the countless lives and communities that continue to be affected.
JNS reports that Israel’s envoy to the Christian world George Deek praised the Flags of Fellowship movement ahead of the annual Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit.
Three years after October 7, to see millions of Christians around the world publicly raise Israel’s flag is a powerful reminder that friendship can speak louder than hatred. More than 5.2 million Israeli flags, over 4,375 churches, universities and organizations, in 14 countries. WOW.
At a time when Israel and the Jewish people have faced extraordinary hatred, millions of Christians are choosing something different: friendship, remembrance and solidarity. I am deeply grateful to the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews, to Yael Eckstein, and to every pastor, church and community taking part in this remarkable initiative.
To our Christian friends around the world: thank you for standing with Israel. We see you. We appreciate you. And we will never take your friendship for granted.
The Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit will run through October 11, coinciding with Flags of Fellowship. More than 1,000 Christian leaders and influencers from 117 countries arrived in Israel on Monday for the second consecutive year of the summit. Around 300 of the participants are between the ages of 18 and 29. Summit founder Mike Evans says he hopes young Christians will see Israel for themselves and hear directly from those affected by October 7.
Much like Flags of Fellowship, the Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit carries the powerful message that Israel does not stand alone, building connections based on truth, courage, and a determination to confront anti-Semitism.
The Fellowship and our supporters pray for the families and remember the victims of October 7 alongside the 4,375 churches and synagogues around the world participating in Flags of Fellowship and the Christian ambassadors who have just arrived in Israel.

articles.title_orig: Paxton’s latest audio leak is making things tough for national Republicans
articles.title_zh: Paxton’s latest audio leak is making things tough for national Republicans
articles.content_orig:
National Republicans have spent months trying to rescue Ken Paxton. He's complicating that effort.
Tensions are brewing with some Republicans after POLITICO published Paxton's closed-door comments that "D.C." Republicans were largely controlling his race .
"He is welcome to raise his own money and say whatever he wants," said one Republican involved in the Paxton rescue effort, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. "In fact, if he did that, he'd probably be winning right now and we wouldn't need to spend all this money."
"This just seems like Paxton preparing to blame others for what might be one of the most embarrassing defeats in modern political history," said Carlos Curbelo, a former Florida GOP representative.
Senate Republicans and top operatives didn't want to be in this position in the first place. Many had warned that the Trump effort to unseat Sen. John Cornyn and back Paxton in the primary would cost Republicans hundreds of millions to drag Paxton across the finish line in the general election. Cornyn and Senate GOP groups spent millions of dollars on ads during the primary attacking Paxton over his series of scandals and warning he was a flawed candidate.
Since then, the usual crowd of never-Paxton types has expanded into a wider circle of frustrated Republicans who are irked by the effort it's taking to boost the scandal-plagued Senate candidate. And Paxton saying he doesn't control his campaign messaging — alongside his remarks that President Donald Trump's midterm convention hurt him politically — isn't helping.
Paxton also complained about the drag of the Iran war and high prices on his campaign in another closed-door recording that Axios published Wednesday .
"Beggars can't be choosers. He can try to raise federal money at a level that is necessary to save his candidacy at this point but his arms don't reach that high," said a Texas-based GOP consultant who's closely monitoring multiple races. "As usual, he communicates something that is unhelpful, that is undisciplined, that is politically self-harmful and like most things, lacks any gratitude whatsoever."
The top Senate GOP super PAC, Trump's aligned MAGA Inc. operation and other Republicans are pumping more than $200 million into the race to salvage Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico. Trump allies say they have worked hard to shore up Paxton, suggesting they've pushed donations toward the campaign and the larger GOP super PAC effort to avoid disaster in the Lone Star State. Trump plans to travel to Texas for the second time Wednesday to boost Paxton.
Paxton allies have brushed off his latest closed-door comments, saying he was referring to GOP super PACs he's not allowed to coordinate with as a candidate.
The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment, though campaign adviser Nick Maddux said in response to POLITICO's initial report of the audio that "AG Paxton is thankful for the support and knows how important Texas is to keeping the majority, which is why he's on the ground every day."
But another Republican, a Trump ally working on the fundraising effort, said the national intervention isn't overstepping. That person said the messaging guidance from the national GOP is standard for major Senate races and that Paxton "needs the help."
One national GOP operative involved in the Texas Senate race noted that the attorney general's lackluster fundraising early on left him vulnerable to Talarico's attacks throughout the summer — especially over Paxton's series of "self-inflicted" scandals, which have made him "toxic" with key voting blocs in the deep red state.
"We warned them about this," the GOP operative said.
The Texas Senate race has sucked up oxygen, despite Trump winning the state in 2024 by double digits. And, the Senate map has kept expanding as Democrats have made gains in other typically red states, forcing Republicans to make critical decisions about where to allocate resources.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Republicans have said there are dedicated donors who are backing their effort to help Paxton, as they also try to shore up red seats across the map.
Paxton, in the September meeting with donors, acknowledged Washington's influence.
"I've never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign … it's all coming — you know — from D.C.," Paxton told donors during a small fundraising event last month, according to the audio.
Top GOP officials have tried to downplay Paxton's comments. The White House referred POLITICO to the RNC when asked for comment. The RNC argued Paxton, in the audio, was referring to the super PACs he can't coordinate with as a candidate.
"This is fake news nonsense mixed with lazy reporting demonstrating a clear ignorance about how super PACs work. President Trump has called Ken Paxton the single greatest attorney general in history and has been clear he will do whatever it takes to make him the next senator from Texas," RNC spokesperson Zach Kraft said in a statement.
Trump, when speaking to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, said he hadn't seen Paxton's latest comments. He added that his midterm travel blitz has helped Paxton and other Republican candidates.
"Ken's doing much better now that I — everybody is — since starting three, four days ago, since starting the rallies. It's brought a whole new awareness to how great the Republicans are doing, how great the economy is doing," Trump said, touting investments and manufacturing.
The president last week traveled to Texas and told the crowd that Paxton is a "pain in the ass sometimes" and later acknowledged he's "a little controversial." But, he also warned the Texas crowd that Talarico would be "such a horror to your state," adding, "we need the votes and I'm here for that, and I think we're going to win."
Vance also traveled to Texas, where he called Paxton an "amazing attorney general and your next senator."
Still, other Republicans have simply grown resigned to the state of the race, with Paxton needing all the aid he can get.
"There is only so much we can do," one senior Senate GOP aide said. "And I feel like we're doing a lot."
The Paxton campaign told POLITICO it raised $18 million in the third quarter across the campaign and his joint fundraising committees. That's roughly double his second-quarter total, though the campaign did not provide its cash-on-hand numbers, and Talarico has yet to release his fundraising haul.
Paxton also announced a $20 million ad buy last week — a significant single media investment in the race. But he's had to rely heavily on Trump, MAGA Inc. and the top Senate GOP super PAC to bail him out.
Republicans have largely leaned on the Senate Leadership Fund, rather than the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. super PAC, to keep Paxton afloat. SLF is spending a Texas record-breaking $131 million sum through Oct. 12 and has pledged to continue to spend more through the final weeks of the election.
MAGA Inc. is increasing some spending for Paxton and is expected to hit near $45 million by Oct. 12.
If Paxton were to lose, Trump's reaction and whether he chooses to distance himself from the rescue effort will be driven by media coverage, said a former Trump fundraiser.
"If the media coverage related to election night and the autopsy a couple days afterwards is brutal towards Trump, like, horrible economy, inflation's not that much better than the last year of Joe Biden's ... he will lash out," the person said. "But if the narrative is, it's a midterm presidential, this is what normally happens … he'll move on as fast as he can and never talk about Ken Paxton again. It just depends what the coverage looks like post the November election."
Myah Ward contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: This ‘Social Reckoning’ arrives way too late
articles.title_zh: This ‘Social Reckoning’ arrives way too late
articles.content_orig:
No matter what you may think of his screenplays overall, Aaron Sorkin writes techies well. He understands the folks entrenched in my former career. His uncanny characterizations worked in Danny Boyle’s 2015 biopic, “Steve Jobs,” and won him an Oscar for 2010’s movie about the origins of Facebook, “The Social Network.” That film also benefited from the dark-hearted directing of David Fincher and the sinister score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.
None of those last three are associated with “The Social Reckoning,” the next chapter in Sorkin’s Mark Zuckerberg Universe. Neither is Jesse Eisenberg, who played Zuckerberg in this film’s predecessor. Jeremy Strong takes over the role as an older, richer, and meaner version of Facebook’s founder. But this time, Zuckerberg’s not the main focus; he’s a supporting character in the story of whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), the Wall Street Journal reporter who published her findings in “The Facebook Files.”
Though I originally had no desire to see a movie about the type of co-workers I endured all day in Silicon Valley, “The Social Network” was my number one movie of 2010. No such fate will befall the somewhat inferior “The Social Reckoning,” though Madison continues Sorkin’s run of pitch perfect techies. She’s socially awkward, incredibly sharp, tuned into details, and impatiently mean and snarky to anyone who doesn’t understand technology. If you ever got the feeling that the folks in your I.T. department hated you, or at the very least, thought you were lesser beings, this former techie is here to say you may not be wrong.
Poor Jeffrey Horwitz learns this lesson the hard way. He’s not tech-savvy, yet he’s applying to cover the Facebook beat for the WSJ. He doesn’t even have a Facebook account, let alone know how to work the GPS that would have gotten him to the job interview on time. His potential boss, Christina (a hilariously tart-tongued Betty Gilpin), is against hiring him, but Jeffrey has an ally in her colleague Andy (Gbenga Akinnagbe), who signs up to be his editor. Christina gives Jeffrey 90 days to get up to speed.
Meanwhile, Frances is at her desk watching an Instagram video of a drunk woman screaming at the two minority cops who noticed her standing outside of her car on the side of a highway. “The Social Reckoning,” which is broken into chapters, opens with the recording of that video after an onscreen credit that reads “Prologue: White Girl Wasted” appears. The White girl in question screams that the cops are DEI hires and is extremely abusive. Once she threatens the cops’ lives, she’s arrested.
Frances recognizes the woman as a former classmate of hers, a woman who just a few years earlier had been extremely progressive in her political views. Now, she’s a raging right-winger who thinks she can abuse minorities with impunity. Sorkin hinges Frances’ decision to research Facebook’s algorithms to see if they distributed ragebait into users’ feeds primarily on her reaction to this woman’s freakout.
It’s a flimsy entry point that I didn’t fully buy. But it does get the plot moving. As a manager in the civics integrity team, Frances discovers that 64 percent of people who joined extremist groups on Facebook were sent to them by the software’s algorithm. When no one listens to her concerns, she responds to the info-seeking Jeffrey’s LinkedIn message. She knows who he is; an internal Facebook meeting has singled him out as a troublemaking journalist to avoid.
Sorkin is careful not to frame Frances as a Facebook hater. Despite being treated like dirt by her sexist male co-workers, she repeatedly states that she loves her job — too many times, if you ask me. She feels that bringing her newfound concerns to Jeffrey will do some good for the company by forcing a few changes. “We are not on the same side,” she tells him. Soon, they’re meeting at some isolated location in a park, as if she’s the Deep Throat to his Woodward in these “All the President’s Men”-inspired scenes. “The Social Reckoning” has a lot of fun with these meetings.
The film hops back and forth in time between 2019, 2020, and 2021. In that last year, we’re privy to Zuckerberg being coached by an agency he’s hired “to make me more likable.” Not even Jesus on His best day could make this incarnation of Zuckerberg pleasant. Strong is delightfully vicious, but he has some strong pushback from “Sinners”’s Wunmi Mosaku as Raya, the frazzled manager trying to help him ace his upcoming congressional testimony, and from Bill Burr as a former adviser turned adversary who’s been hired by Raya to get under Zuckerberg’s skin in these practice sessions.
As you’d expect from Sorkin, “The Social Reckoning” is a very talky movie that tends to overexplain itself. He even throws in a “walk with me” line for fans of “The West Wing.” It’s not enough for Jeffrey to be the audience’s stand-in as Frances painstakingly explains all her data to him; we need others to explain things, too. I wasn’t too bothered by this, as everyone in the cast is very good. Madison, in particular, is excellent, better than she was in “Anora.” White is a good comedic scene partner, bouncing off her barbs with good humor and genuine interest.
My biggest problem with “The Social Reckoning” is that it feels like too little, too late. Had this come out three years ago, it would have felt more timely and relevant. As it stands, the film isn’t telling us anything we don’t already know, and the social media problems are even bigger and more destructive than they were in this movie’s timeline. The film also aims the onus of blame on algorithms and not the people radicalized by them. Watching this film, you’d think Facebook was turning nice little progressives and liberals into rabid racists, homophobes, and white supremacists. All those algorithms did was push people off ledges they were already standing on of their own volition. These people aren’t blameless innocents.
Written and directed by Aaron Sorkin. Starring Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Jeremy Strong, Betty Gilpin, Wunmi Mosaku, Bill Burr, Gbenga Akinnagbe. At AMC Boston Common, Landmark Kendall Square, Alamo Drafthouse Seaport, AMC Causeway, suburbs. 112 minutes. R (language)
Odie Henderson is the Boston Globe's film critic.
